items.question: How do I calm down and wait on God so I can hear from Him?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this directly. Calming down is itself the way the greatest miracle was stirred up — Jesus had the agitated crowd sit down, and the word to you is, "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God" (Philippians 4:6) [1]. A flustered person running from one emergency to another will not think clearly or hear from God, and sometimes it takes several days to calm down — the Levites stayed at the tabernacle door seven days for their consecration [1].

Waiting on God is a skill few have, and if you do not wait on God you will not hear from Him; they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength (Isaiah 40:31), and when Paul and the prophets waited and ministered to the Lord, the Holy Spirit spoke and launched the mission to the ends of the world [4]. Silence helps you hear from God — "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psalm 46:10) — for many do not hear Him because they are too busy talking, chatting or singing [2]. You can also set yourself targets, giving yourself a number of hours to pray, as Jesus continued all night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12) [5], and time yourself, noting when you start and deciding how long you will pray, for Jesus asked Peter, "What, could ye not watch with me one hour?" (Matthew 26:40) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Stir It Up*, chapter 12 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*, chapter 9 of *The Privilege* and chapter 24 of *Church Growth*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 46:10; Isaiah 40:31; Daniel 1:4; Joel 2:15-17; Matthew 26:40; Luke 6:12; Acts 13:1-2; Philippians 4:6.

items.question: Why is it dangerous to pretend to be strong when I'm actually struggling?
items.text:
It's dangerous because pretending keeps you from the help you need. If your pastor knows you are weak, he can pray for you, but if you pretend to be mighty, how can he know you need help? [1][2] When you appear strong even though you are weak, nobody can help you, and you are preventing your own deliverance by covering what needs help [1][2].

The picture given is Samson: mighty in ministry, killing thousands, yet weak in his private life — mighty publicly but the opposite in private [1][2]. And as a pastor, there are people he doesn't particularly need to visit because they are strong, but when there is a weak one he rushes there because that one needs attention; when you look strong like Samson, you won't get any attention [1][2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Duality* and chapter 11 of *Spiritual Dangers*.

items.question: What mistakes do pastors usually make that hurt their ministry?
items.book: The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make
items.text:
Friend, our books name several mistakes that wound a ministry. Choosing to bear little fruit is one of them — leaving a fruitful place for somewhere with no one to preach to, when God is glorified by much fruit, as John 15:8 says [1]. Turning into a Pharisee is another, loving the chief seats and greetings in the markets, as Matthew 23:6-7 describes [2]. Wrong priorities kill a ministry too: not building your own church while you run after invitations and honorariums, or giving priority to the rich and powerful while setting aside the young, the children and the poor [4].

There is also being slow about ministry, slow to obey the call of God, when speed matters [7]. And downplaying humility — pastors who are no longer like little children, unable to be taught, unwilling to lift a hand or say Amen, though Matthew 18:3 says we must become as little children [8]. Disappointing shepherds, the books add, choose their own sacrifices instead of obeying, stop seeing themselves as sheep needing direction, and fail to remain small in their own eyes, as 1 Samuel 15:16-17 shows with Saul [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 3, 7, 8 and 9 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make* and chapter 31 of *The Art of Shepherding*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:16-17; Matthew 18:3; Matthew 23:6-7; John 7:6; John 15:8.

items.question: Why do people hear the same sermon differently?
items.text:
People hear the same sermon differently because, as Jesus said, "their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed" (Matthew 13:15) [1]. Some only hear your accent, some the grammar, some the stories or jokes, while others hear the principles and Scriptures, and still others hear the Spirit speaking and receive wisdom and guidance from the Holy Spirit [1]. Jesus knew people were hearing differently, which is why He said, "Hearing they cannot hear" [1].

Hearing properly is to hear with faith, for the word preached profits only when it is "mixed with faith in them that heard it" (Hebrews 4:1-2) [8]. Judas sat at the table when Jesus said one of them would betray Him, yet the message did not benefit him because he did not hear with faith (Luke 22:22-23) [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 12 of *Steps to the Anointing* and chapter 16 of *Seeing And Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 4:7; Matthew 13:14-15; Luke 22:22-23; Hebrews 4:1-2.

items.question: Why is my church not growing?
items.book: Why Is This Church Not Working?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this weight, pastor. Our books name several possible reasons, and I'd gently lay them before you.

Your church may not be growing because you have a low capacity for studying — people who do not study books on ministry and church growth will not have growth, and a failing church is a revelation of a lack of knowledge, wisdom and understanding [2]. It may be that you are not diligent, passive and laid-back, needing constant supervision, for pastors who make a constant effort to accomplish something are the only ones who have working churches [3]. It may be the location: you are not supposed to worship just anywhere, but in the place which the Lord shall choose (Deuteronomy 12:13-14), and perhaps it is time you relocated your church [4]. It may be that you are using the wrong church growth strategy, for a house is built through wisdom and by a series of steps (Proverbs 24:3-4) [5]. Or it may be that your vision is not a burning vision, for in the absence of a burning vision for a large church you will never have real church growth [7].

Alongside these, the books also say church growth is warfare — something is fighting you, that is why your church is not growing, and pastors who are not prepared to go to war cannot have church growth [1]. And they say the beginning of a church is like a mustard seed (Matthew 13:31-32), so don't be in a hurry; there isn't any tree that grows from a seed into a large tree overnight [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church*, chapters 11, 12, 17 and 18 of *Why Is This Church Not Working?*, chapter 1 of *Church Growth* and chapter 7 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 12:13-14; Proverbs 22:29; Proverbs 24:3-4; Proverbs 29:18; Matthew 13:31-32; Mark 6:2; 2 Timothy 2:15.

items.question: What diseases can you get from having sex before marriage?
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this. Fornication—sexual intercourse before marriage [3][5]—can bring sickness: the germs that cause sexually transmitted diseases gain access into you when you commit fornication, and the books list ten of them, including Gonorrhoea, Syphilis, Non-Specific Urethritis, liver diseases from Hepatitis B, Herpes Genitalis, Vaginitis, Lymphogranuloma venereum, Soft Sore (Chancroid), urinary tract infection, and cancer of the cervix, which frequent sex at an early age predisposes you to [1][2].

Fornication can also bring death: it will kill you if you acquire the Human Immuno Virus (HIV), and unless God works a miracle, you may die of AIDS [1][2]. The books add that HIV is now a death sentence, and sadly there are many Christians in charismatic churches who are HIV positive—so fornicating with your fellow church member may mean your death [2]. If you wait till you marry before having sex, you may save yourself from all these diseases [1][2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Spiritual Dangers* and chapters 2 and 3 of *All About Fornication*.

Scriptures referenced: Jeremiah 3:15; Ephesians 5:3.

items.question: How can I know if I'm on the wrong path in life?
items.text:
Our books speak to this in a few ways. One test is the company on the road: the broad way has many people on it and the narrow way has few, and it is the road with a lot of people that the world sees as the right road — yet Jesus warned that you must be among the few who choose Him [2]. Another test is your conscience, that quiet inner voice that checks you when you go wrong; your heart can condemn you for wrongdoing, and anyone who claims to be led by the Spirit but ignores his conscience is headed for tragedy [4].

The books also warn that a way can seem right and still end in death, as Proverbs 14:12 says [7], and that the ways of heaping up riches or of pleasure are not the way to God [7]. And when you are unsure, safety lies in a multitude of counsellors and in proving all things, as 1 Thessalonians 5:21 says — subject every voice to the Word of God [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 50 and 65 of *How You Can Preach Salvation* and chapters 23 and 24 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 14:12; Ecclesiastes 4:8; Matthew 7:13-14; John 14:4-6; Acts 24:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:21; 1 John 3:20-21.

items.question: What should I do when one of them is a leader I trained?
items.text:
When a leader you trained departs, our books speak plainly. If someone indicates a desire to leave, it is best for such a person not to stay on but to leave immediately, because his heart has already left the church [8]. The reason given is that "a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6), and after Judas resigned from Jesus' ministry, Jesus told him, "That thou doest, do quickly" (John 13:27) [8]. One dissenting employee pollutes the others with his disgruntled attitude [8].

If he must resign, he should resign alone and not try to influence other ministers to leave with him [1]. He should not win the hearts of people long beforehand by making special friends and developing close relationships with vital church members, for in the end he leaves behind a confused group of members who must choose between their relationship with him and their commitment to the church [1]. If he intends to set up a church, he must declare his intentions to the senior minister, and he must discourage others from following him [1][2]. He should not set up a church anywhere within a ten-mile radius from where he used to be [1][2]. And he should be grateful to the church he is leaving and not spread bad stories about it, for "Whoso rewardeth evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house" (Proverbs 17:13) [1][2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*, chapter 4 of *Ministerial Ethics* and chapter 3 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 10 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapter 4 of *Ministerial Ethics*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 17:13; Ezekiel 34:18; John 13:27; 1 Corinthians 5:6.

items.question: What does it mean to build a church on a deep foundation?
items.text:
Building a church on a deep foundation means going deeper so you can build something great for God — tall, majestic structures are only possible by going deeper [1]. Jesus told of the man who dug deep and laid his foundation on a rock, so that when the flood beat against the house it could not shake it, because it was founded on a rock (Luke 6:47-49) [1]. The deeper and stronger the foundation, the greater and taller the building [2].

Those foundations include salvation through the blood and cross of Jesus Christ, faithfulness and loyalty, evangelism and outreach, teaching and sticking to the word of God, tithes and offerings as the financing for God's work, and the truth that God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son (John 3:16) [1][2]. These must be deeply rooted and never set aside, and they must be protected — as Psalm 11:3 asks, "If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?" [2][3][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Going Deeper and Doing More*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 11:3; Luke 6:47-49.

items.question: What does it mean when someone constantly accuses others and tries to control them?
items.text:
When someone constantly accuses others and tries to control them, the books describe this as witchcraft — the use of any power other than the power of God to control people [1]. One way of establishing control is to accuse and pester someone with words; through persistent accusations, controlling people stop you from doing certain things they do not like, and this kind of witchcraft is not easy to recognize [1]. A person with a controlling spirit is a witch, and such a person wields this power through relentless accusations [2].

The books also say accusations are manifestations of hatred, and that your accuser is the one who hates you most [2]. Accusations are perfect tools to control great people, and they harass and threaten God's servants [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 4 of *Those Who Accuse You*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 25:24-25; John 15:25.

items.question: What are creeping things in the spiritual sense and how do I pray against them in my church?
items.text:
Creeping things are things that sneak up on you without you realising it — great changes that take place over a long period of time, so that most people hardly notice them happening [2]. The book names four that creep upon all churches: deception, wrong attitudes like laziness, complacency and unbelief, familiarity, and the shifting of priorities, such as becoming health and educational organisations instead of missionary societies [2]. Deception is the clearest example — the church in Europe did not degenerate overnight; the spirit of deception crept on it slowly [1][2].

As for praying against them, the book says intercessory prayer is necessary to keep out these spiritual creepers, and that intercessory prayer will fight the creeping familiarity that kills the flow of the Spirit [1]. It also points to the dominion God gave man over every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth (Genesis 1:25, 26) [2]. Beyond that, our books have not directly addressed this.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 21 of *Transform Your Pastoral Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 1:25-26.

items.question: How do I start a new church in a town where we have no members?
items.text:
What a good and honest question, and our books speak directly to it. You do not need a crowd to begin — two or three is enough, for where two or three are gathered in His name, there He is in the midst of them (Matthew 18:20) [6]. One pastor who knew nobody in South Africa started a church there, and the Lighthouse Cathedral began with as few as five people [6]. If you are truly called of God, the only person you need is yourself [6].

Count the cost first, as Luke 14:28 says, sitting down before you build the tower [5]. Start in an honourable way — the art of beginning a church is witnessing, following up and gathering sheep, and you do not need to break up someone else's church to do it [5]. Do not be financially desperate in these early stages; find a job and start as a lay person, for a small church usually cannot pay a pastor's salary [1][2]. And do not be discouraged by small or fluctuating numbers — that is how sheep behave; take no notice of them [3][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 20 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 18:20; Luke 14:28.

items.question: What does the Bible say about being a shepherd like Jesus?
items.text:
Being a shepherd is a privilege, not just a job — Jesus Himself was a shepherd, and He called Himself the Good Shepherd (John 10:11), so you are joining Him in His chosen profession [1]. A shepherd is a caring, loving guide whom God has called to look after His sheep [5], and the work involves visiting people, praying for them, counselling with the word of God, preaching and teaching [1].

Jesus described what a good shepherd does in John 10. A good shepherd leads his sheep, being practically available so they can see and learn from him — anything you want your sheep to do, you must first do it yourself [2][7]. He also goes after the lost: He leaves the ninety-nine and searches for the one lost sheep, and that is what makes him a good shepherd (Luke 15:4-7) [4]. So a good shepherd seeks to save sinners, since Jesus said He came to seek and save that which was lost (Luke 19:10) [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *The Privilege*, chapters 1, 9 and 13 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapter 2 of *How You Can Preach Salvation* and chapter 8 of *Church Growth*.

items.question: How does the grace of God help my ministry reach more people and get support?
items.book: How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry
items.text:
The grace of God is what makes your gift available to many people — it's why some ministries have great patronage, many readers, and many supporters [1]. It's also the grace of God that causes much support to abound toward your ministry; when great grace was upon the early church, no one among them lacked, and they sold their possessions and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet (Acts 4:33-35) [1].

The grace of God also determines how far your ministry will go — it's why some pastors have larger churches and others smaller, why some evangelists have larger crowds [2]. And it can be seen by the great numbers who respond: when Barnabas came to Antioch and saw the grace of God, a great number had believed and turned to the Lord (Acts 11:19-24) [3]. So pray for the grace of God to work powerfully in your life and ministry [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 17 of *How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Acts 4:33-35; 2 Timothy 1:8-9; 2 Timothy 2:1; Titus 2:11-12.

items.question: What is true forgiveness?
items.text:
True forgiveness is releasing all hurts, bitterness, and wickedness from your heart, so that you give up all claims against the one who offended you, cancel any indebtedness, make no more mention of the matter, stop feeling resentment and anger, and cancel any punishment you had planned for them [7]. It is choosing to let go and release the grudge, so that you are liberated [1]. A real test of it is being able to pray sincerely for the well-being of the one who hurt you [1].

The Lord also taught that genuine forgiveness and the prayer for God to avenge you go together, leaving vengeance to Him, for "Vengeance is mine, says the Lord" (Romans 12:19) [3][5]. And forgiveness makes you a great person, as Psalm 130:4 says, "there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared" [6].

items.question: What happens spiritually to a Christian who commits fornication?
items.text:
When a Christian commits fornication, the Bible says he destroys his own soul — Proverbs 6:32 says the one who does it destroys his own soul [1][2]. It has a real effect on you spiritually, even if you cannot say exactly how; it affects you and leads you to backslide, and with experience the writer has seen a person's spiritual life take a nosedive and their lifestyle change when they fall into immorality [1][2].

It is also disobedience to God, and obedience means more to Him than any sacrifice you can make — as 1 Samuel 15:22 says, "to obey is better than sacrifice" [7]. And it is not only the soul: you sin directly against your own body, as 1 Corinthians 6:18 says, "he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body" [1][2][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Spiritual Dangers* and chapter 3 of *All About Fornication*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:22; Proverbs 6:32; 1 Corinthians 6:15; 1 Corinthians 6:18-19.

items.question: How do I get my life ready to die?
items.text:
What a good and sober question. The books say plainly that to set your house in order is to get ready for death and eternity, and that this command is given to all of us, not only to Hezekiah [1]. They also say a strong Christian is ready to meet God at any time, and that you can only be ready through the blood of Jesus who died for you [8].

One way they describe getting ready is to prepare for the gospel and preach it for the rest of your life, since what you did with the gospel and whether you served the Lord will matter greatly in eternity [1]. They also speak of being ready in every season, not waiting for the twilight of your life, because Scripture teaches us to be ready in season and out of season (2 Timothy 4:2) [3]. And they hold up the example of Christ, who acted responsibly even while facing imminent death and could say, "it is finished" — the only way to die the death of a righteous person is to fulfil your ministry [6].

The books also urge a practical readiness: a good general prepares for the reality of death and has an escape plan, asking what will happen to your church if you die [5]. And they warn that it is not safe to assume there is more time, for we do not know the day or the hour, so the key word is preparation and readiness (Amos 4:12) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 11 and 12 of *The Preparation of the Gospel*, chapter 47 of *A Good General*, chapter 10 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 4 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: Daniel 12:3; Amos 4:12; Luke 12:1-59; Romans 1:15-16; 1 Thessalonians 4:16-18; 2 Timothy 4:2.

Please also speak with your shepherd or pastor today. Where a life may be at risk, contact emergency services or a medical professional now.

items.question: How do I get closer to God through apostles, prophets, pastors, teachers and evangelists?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly. They say people do not become close to God until they accept apostles, prophets, pastors, teachers and evangelists, because these are doors for you into His presence [1]. The writer says he became closer to God by accepting great prophets and pastors into his life, and that you cannot go far without true apostles and prophets, nor get far without a pastor, a teacher or an evangelist [1].

They also warn that when people say, "Do not trust a man," or "Be careful of these money-grabbing men of God," what is actually happening is that you are being driven away from the five-pillared door to the presence of God [1]. And these men are God's gift to you — as Ephesians 4:11 says, He gave gifts unto men: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers — so be thankful for the servants God has sent you, rather than discontented with them [4].

One caution the books add: judge what is said, for 1 Corinthians 14:29 tells us the declarations of prophets are to be assessed, and the Word of God is the standard by which we assess them [3]. A true prophet will be known by his fruits; if the end result of a ministry is destabilization and members being moved to and fro, that is not the fruit of a New Testament prophet, for as Ephesians 4:11,14 shows, these gifts are given so the saints are no longer children tossed to and fro [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 18 of *Steps to God's Presence*, chapter 18 of *The Art of Hearing* and chapter 1 of *How Can I Say Thanks*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Corinthians 14:29; Ephesians 4:11-14; 1 Thessalonians 5:12.

items.question: How can I stay focused and really connect with God when I pray instead of getting distracted or falling asleep?
items.text:
Friend, this is a struggle the books speak to directly, and you're not alone in it.

One help is to build an atmosphere where you can see and hear from God while you pray — the author describes playing anointed videos and music during his prayer time, saying that when such a video is playing it is as though you are part of a miracle service, and that he has enjoyed the power of God spending hours in prayer this way [1]. He also warns that a cold, silent room with only polluted television left him hardly able to pray, so he never allowed himself to be anywhere without the ability to create that atmosphere [1].

Distractions can also be cut off deliberately: disconnect your phone, because needless interruptions break your precious hour of prayer into piecemeal five-minute sessions, and issuing a "do not disturb" notice to those you live with helps, just as they wouldn't disturb you in the bathroom [2].

As for sleep, the books treat watching — staying awake to pray — as central: "watch and pray" means stay awake and pray, and learning to overcome sleep by going to bed early so you can rise a great while before day was the life of Jesus, who rose up a great while before day and prayed (Mark 1:35) [3]. David Yonggi Cho prayed three to five hours daily for over thirty years, and waking at night to watch and pray was his secret [3]. Inappropriate sleep also renders you defenceless, as with Saul's sleeping guards [3]. Jesus Himself was surprised the disciples could not watch with Him one hour (Matthew 26:40) [4].

Finally, quiet-time prayer alone builds a very personal relationship with God — many can only pray in a group, and expanding your ability to pray alone expands your ability to achieve great things in prayer [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Seeing And Hearing*, chapter 10 of *Transform Your Pastoral Ministry*, chapter 3 of *Awake, O Sleeper* and chapter 8 of *The Secret*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 26:36-40; Matthew 26:42-44; Mark 1:35; Luke 6:12-13.

items.question: People are spreading lies about me in the church. How should I respond?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this. Our books speak directly to slander, and they say a slanderer spreads fear and panic through their stories, so that many feel the church is collapsing because of words like these [4]. But God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love and a sound mind, as 2 Timothy 1:7 says [4]. The psalmist faced the same thing and said, "I trusted in thee, O Lord: I said, Thou art my God" (Psalm 31:11-14) [4].

The books also warn that slander is evil because it spreads the failings of a brother, and that a slanderer reveals secrets while a trustworthy person conceals a matter, as Proverbs 11:13 says [7]. People who fall are to be helped up, not pushed further down [7]. And where a leader is the one slandering, the books say that authority gives credence to the stories being peddled, which makes it especially dangerous [1].

One thing the books do not settle for you: they describe both enduring slander with trust in God [4] and, in another place, correcting and even dismissing a scorner so that strife ceases, as Proverbs 22:10 says [5]. They present both, and I won't choose between them for you.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Those Who Are Slanderers* and chapter 11 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 31:11-14; Psalms 105:15; Psalms 119:21-24; Proverbs 11:13; Proverbs 22:10; 1 Corinthians 5:6-7; 2 Timothy 1:7; Jude 22.

items.question: Why do some Christians who give tithes prosper while others struggle?
items.book: Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich
items.text:
The books speak to this directly. Tithing is a seed sown in the house of God, and everyone who sows qualifies for a harvest — "they that sow in tears shall reap in joy" (Psalm 126:5), and "give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over" (Luke 6:38) [3]. Tithing also fulfils the law of humility, since it makes you bow before your Creator and recognise that you did not make it on your own [5][6].

But the books also name reasons why tithing does not seem to work for some. Hidden sin can cancel the blessing, for "he that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy" (Proverbs 28:13) [1]. Wrong desires do the same, since "ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts" (James 4:2-3) [4]. Strife with the brethren hinders it, for "the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace" (James 3:18) [4]. And troubled marriages neutralize prayers, as 1 Peter 3:7 says, that your prayers "be not hindered" [1][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 14 and 22 of *Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 75:6-7; Psalms 126:5; Proverbs 28:13; Matthew 6:33; Luke 6:38; James 3:18; James 4:2-3; 1 Peter 3:7.

items.question: How can a husband help his wife stay beautiful?
items.text:
A husband has a real part to play here, and the books speak to it plainly. Beauty depends on many factors, so invest in those factors — a wife's beauty depends on her hair, her dressing, her make-up, and even the time of day [3]. As a good husband, be concerned about which dress your wife wears, because her beauty also depends on her dressing [2][3]. Tell her how you like her hair and how to do it; since you are her husband, she desires to please you [3]. Beauty also depends on money — the more you have, the more you can invest in making your wife beautiful, so here is another reason for a Christian husband to prosper [2]. You will reap what you sow: if you sow into your wife's clothes, you will reap great dividends [3].

And it is for your own good: the man is presenting the woman back to himself, so it is to his own benefit to nourish, cherish and beautify his wife [4], as Ephesians 5:25-29 says, no man ever yet hated his own flesh but nourisheth and cherisheth it [4]. Let her feel loved, wanted and accepted [4]. One caution: do not make scathing remarks about your wife's body, for instance comments like "Your stomach is too big" — but speaking the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), and so ought men to love their wives as their own bodies (Ephesians 5:28) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Beauty* and chapters 11 and 32 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 5:18; Ecclesiastes 9:9; 1 Corinthians 11:15; Ephesians 4:15; Ephesians 5:25-29; Colossians 3:19.

items.question: What does the Bible say about wasting opportunities?
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this. One way people lose good opportunities is by being extravagant—living beyond your means and spending in excess is a waste of good opportunity [1]. The prodigal son "wasted his substance with riotous living" (Luke 15:11-14), and among the opportunities he wasted was the chance to benefit from his father's advice [1][2]. The road to lost opportunities begins with separation—separating yourself from God and from fellowship, as the son did when he journeyed into a far country (Luke 15:13) [3].

There is also a stewardship side to it: if you waste what God has put into your hand, you will lose your valued position, for the steward was told, "thou mayest be no longer steward" (Luke 16:1-2) [5]. And greed can squander great opportunities too—Gehazi's opportunity was denied him because of the spirit of greed (2 Kings 5:27) [6]. On the other side, the one who "hath" does not waste the opportunity to win souls, remembering that a soul is worth more than the whole world (Matthew 16:26) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 4 and 10 of *Opportunities* and chapter 14 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Kings 5:27; Matthew 16:26; Luke 15:11-14; Luke 16:1-2; 1 Thessalonians 5:12-13.

items.question: How should a church deal with sin and rebellion among its leaders?
items.text:
Our books speak to this plainly. Sin must not be trivialized or dealt with lightly; when someone has to be dismissed, he must be dismissed, and a step of judgment, rejection, dismissal, suspension or removal must be taken, otherwise the organization will begin to decline and an irreversible corruption sets in [1]. At the same time, God combines judgment and restoration very well, so we must master both the official rejection of sin and the official pardoning of sin — a pardon being the official granting of forgiveness for an offence committed by a bishop, pastor or church leader [1].

Rebellion is a unique sin, distinct from every other, and rebels are described as evil men who seek only rebellion (Proverbs 17:11) [3]. You must reject rebels and abhor those in rebellion (Psalm 139:21), not admiring them or using a rebellion as a good example, lest you become a rebel yourself [2]. Scripture even compares rebellion to witchcraft (1 Samuel 15:23), and all who are moved to rebel are headed for destruction [7]. A slanderer is likewise a rebellious person (Jeremiah 6:28), and such rebellious leavers are often the worst slanderers [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 79 of *The Gift Of Governments*, chapter 8 of *Those Who Rebel*, chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 5 of *Those Who Are Slanderers*.

Scriptures referenced: Joshua 22:19; Joshua 24:19; 1 Samuel 15:23; 1 Kings 16:31; Nehemiah 9:17; Job 7:21; Job 34:37; Psalms 139:21; Proverbs 17:11; Jeremiah 6:28.

Rebellion is a unique sin, distinct from every other, and rebels are described as evil men who seek only rebellion (Proverbs 17:11).
You must reject rebels and abhor those in rebellion (Psalm 139:21), not admiring them or using a rebellion as a good example, lest you become a rebel yourself.
Scripture even compares rebellion to witchcraft (1 Samuel 15:23), and all who are moved to rebel are headed for destruction.
A slanderer is likewise a rebellious person (Jeremiah 6:28), and such rebellious leavers are often the worst slanderers.

items.question: How do I stay filled with the Holy Spirit?
items.book: The Sweet Influences of the Anointing
items.text:
What a good thing to long for. Our books say that being filled with the Spirit is stirred up in very ordinary, daily ways.

Prayer meetings bring down the presence of the Holy Spirit — the early church was filled when they prayed, and "every prayer meeting brings us nearer the throne room of the Lord" [1]. Speak to yourself in psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord, for Ephesians 5:18-19 tells us this is how Christians are continually filled [1]. Let that music come from the heart, not from hastily put-together lyrics designed to impress [3]. Give thanks always and for all things (Ephesians 5:18-20); thankfulness causes you to be filled with the Holy Spirit, while criticism and murmuring open you to evil spirits [3][4]. And be humble, submitting yourself to others in the fear of God, for being filled is closely linked to submissiveness and humility [2].

You can also stir up hunger by talking and preaching about the Holy Spirit, for "blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled" (Matthew 5:6), and by asking specifically for Him, since the Father gives the Holy Spirit to them that ask Him [5]. Flow with Him as a real person — talk with Him, listen for His advice, recognize His gentle pressures and sudden gusts as wind [6] — and thirst for Him as water that refreshes and makes you grow like a watered garden (Psalm 63:1, Isaiah 58:11) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 31 of *The Sweet Influences of the Anointing*, chapter 3 of *Those Who Forget* and chapters 1 and 7 of *Flow in the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 63:1; Isaiah 58:11; Matthew 5:6; John 20:22; Acts 2:2; Acts 4:31; Ephesians 5:18-21; 2 Timothy 1:6.

items.question: What does the Bible say about pastors criticizing or attacking other pastors and ministries?
items.book: The Church Must Send or It Will End
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this, and they do not approve of it. Pastors who attack and criticize one another are told to leave other ministers to God, because His judgment is greater than your criticism of them, and your own ministry can come to an end because of your attack on another person's ministry [2]. When pastors deride and denigrate other ministers, the question is whether they are building or destroying the Body, and the warning is: do not break down somebody's house in order to build yours, for you will only reap what you sow [4].

The passages also describe the fruit of this. Constant analysis, criticism and mockery of fellow ministers is common in the conversation of some pastors, and attacking and killing your own brother is a very bad sign and a cause for concern [3]. When the fruits are broken churches, destroyed ministries and deceived pastors, the Spirit of God is not at work; the devil and the flesh are on the rampage [1]. Instead, we are urged to concentrate on the Great Commission and the harvest of souls [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 5 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapter 4 of *The Church Must Send or It Will End* and chapter 8 of *Those who are Dangerous Sons*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 4:8-12; 2 Samuel 13:28; 2 Samuel 14:28.

items.question: A leader I trained for years has just left the church. How do I handle it?
items.text:
I'm sorry — that is a heavy thing to carry, and the books speak to it plainly.

First, know that this is not new under the sun. One pastor trained a man, appointed him, and then watched him leave, plant a church nearby, and "virtually build his church by dividing ours" [8]. Another senior pastor returned from travel to find his associate had resigned and taken almost the whole church — three thousand members reduced to twenty [2]. So your grief is real, and it has been walked before.

On handling it: the books say to remove disloyal people quickly, because "a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6), and after Judas resigned, Jesus told him, "That thou doest, do quickly" (John 13:27) [7]. They also say to bind a "Judas" — to restrict him rather than let him operate freely — and that failing to do so is making yourself wiser than God [2]. And they say to exert your authority and confront disloyalty directly rather than gossip behind his back, since weak leaders who avoid confrontation end up with a worse crisis [5].

But hear the other side too, because the books hold both. They also say to cleanse yourself of the seeds of hurt, anger, hatred and revenge that a departure leaves in your spirit, praying long and hard, lest you fall into bitterness and unforgiveness [4]. And they say God can use even this: each person who leaves can become a stepping stone to a higher dimension of ministry [5], and sometimes a departure "heralds the arrival of God's choice for you" — as David was revealed only when Saul's heart departed [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 33 of *Victory Secrets*, chapters 1 and 10 of *Those who leave you*, chapter 3 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapter 4 of *Those Who Forget*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 16:3; Numbers 16:8-9; 1 Kings 11:3-4; Psalms 141:9-10; Proverbs 3:7; John 13:27; 1 Corinthians 5:6; 1 Corinthians 14:33; 2 Corinthians 7:11.

items.question: How can a pastor's wife support her husband's ministry if she's quiet and doesn't connect with people?
items.book: The Beauty The Beast and The Pastor
items.text:
The books speak directly to this. A wife who is helpful is a quiet and effective backbone to any minister, and many ministers depend on their wives for the quiet and effective help they give [2]. That help is pictured as the salt of the earth — quiet and effective, working behind the scenes, like a helps minister whose influence is real even when the general public does not see or know them [1][2].

So quietness is not the same as disconnection. The books warn that isolation and non-communicative behaviour are a serious flaw and a serious mistake in ministry, and that you will never be made perfect without the input of others, as Hebrews 11:40 says [5]. They also say the body increases through what every joint supplies, and that the eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of thee," as 1 Corinthians 12:20-21 says [5]. A quiet and effective helper is still a joint that supplies.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *Am I Good For Nothing?* and chapter 4 of *Why Is This Church Not Working?*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 2:18; Matthew 6:3-4; Romans 12:8; 1 Corinthians 12:20-21; 1 Corinthians 12:28; Hebrews 11:40.

items.question: How should I respond when people I've loved and helped turn against me?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this. It's a pain every shepherd meets, and our books speak to it plainly.

Don't be surprised by it. Jesus Himself was repaid with stones for His good works (John 10:32), and every leader comes face to face with ingratitude [1]. People you loved can turn and hurt you, and men you trained may not remember the help they were given [1]. Some repay love by becoming adversaries — David wrote, "For my love they are my adversaries: but I give myself unto prayer" (Psalms 109:1-5) [4]. So do not look to people for gratitude; look to God for your reward, for "whatsoever good thing any man doeth, the same shall he receive of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:8) [1].

Two things the books hold side by side. David's response was to pray for God's judgment on those who repaid his good with evil, asking that they be clothed with shame and dishonour (Psalms 35:21-26; 109:5-13) [2][3]. And Jesus, though hurt and broken by Judas, went to the cross thinking of the purposes of God and not the treachery — He never mentioned Judas again, and He was not turned away from His mission by the hurts of ministry [8]. Do not let offences turn you from your mission; keep moving, and learn to forgive because you have been forgiven a lot [8]. If you retaliate because of ingratitude, you will lose your place in the ministry [1].

There is also this comfort: sometimes the departure of a person heralds the arrival of God's choice for you, as David was revealed when Saul's heart departed [7]. Do not struggle when people are taken away; sometimes it is in your eternal destiny that they be taken away and replaced [6]. Walking in love and maturity toward those who desert or turn against you is part of becoming a father [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 101 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 3 of *How Can I Say Thanks*, chapters 1 and 10 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 5 of *Why Few Are Chosen*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 35:21-26; Psalms 109:1-13; Luke 15:11-13; John 10:32; John 21:15-17; Ephesians 6:8; 1 John 2:18-19.

items.question: What does the cross mean for me as a Christian?
items.text:
The cross is the true symbol of Christianity, and every time you see it you are reminded of what it stands for [3]. It is the symbol of the death you must experience, for when Jesus told us to carry our cross He was telling us to go to a place where we would die and lose our lives, as He said in Luke 9:23 [4]. It is also the symbol of the price Christians must pay, for as 1 Corinthians 6:20 says, you were bought with a price [1].

It is the symbol of the love of God you must emulate, since 1 John 3:16 says that as He laid down His life for us, we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren [1]. It is the symbol of obedience, for Philippians 2:8 tells us He humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross [1][5]. And it is the symbol of the sacrifice all of us must make to serve the Lord [1][5].

Taking up your cross also releases power in your life: it has the power to put away sins, and to make you die to sin and live to righteousness [6]. It enables you to enter into a new life of faith and ministry, as Paul said, "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 15 and 17 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying*.

Scriptures referenced: Luke 9:23; 1 Corinthians 6:20; Ephesians 5:2; Philippians 2:8; Colossians 1:20; Hebrews 2:9; Hebrews 9:24-26; 1 John 3:16.

items.question: How do I stop needing people's approval and praise after I preach?
items.text:
What a good and freeing question. The books speak to this directly.

Do not look to people for gratitude or approval; a leader looks to God for rewards, for "whatsoever good thing any man doeth, the same shall he receive of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:8) [1]. Your rewards depend on God, not on the people you helped, so expect your rewards from God rather than from men [1]. One minister described how he stopped expecting people to commend him after preaching, and when he decided not to look for man's approval he felt a sense of liberty, free from men and accountable to the Lord [1].

The same counsel appears elsewhere: you do not need the approval of men, so do not worry about what people think of you — just make sure God thinks highly of you, and you will become a workman who is not ashamed (2 Timothy 2:15-16) [2]. People may congratulate you, but it is the Lord's approval you really need [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 101 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 9 of *The Preparation of the Gospel* and chapter 2 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: John 3:16; John 10:32; Ephesians 6:8; 2 Timothy 2:15-16; 2 Timothy 4:1-2.

items.question: How can I learn to pray early in the morning before my day gets busy?
items.book:
Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer
items.text:
What a good desire, pastor. The books speak directly to this. Jesus Himself rose "a great while before day" and went to a solitary place to pray (Mark 1:35), and you are invited to learn how to do the same [1]. One practical step they give is to go to bed early so that you can rise a great while before day — that was the life of Jesus [3].

They also frame it as a habit worth building: praying at dawn is very repeatable, something you can do tomorrow and every day of the year, even on your busiest days [1]. And they warn that life in the secular world is not designed to include a prayer time, so you must deliberately include it [5][7]. If you can pray for three hours on your own, you can pray for six with others, so expanding your private prayer expands your capacity [4][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*, chapter 3 of *Awake, O Sleeper*, chapter 8 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day* and chapter 1 of *How to Pray*.

Scriptures referenced: Daniel 6:10; Matthew 26:36-40; Mark 1:34-36; Luke 4:16; Luke 6:12-13.

items.question: How can I pray for the sick and be a source of healing?
items.text:
You can become a source of healing simply by praying for the sick — God is interested in the sick and suffering, and through your prayers healing and deliverance come to many [1]. Jesus said He was anointed to heal the broken-hearted, and many people are comforted when hands are laid on them [1].

Don't be afraid to step out. Every opportunity to pray for the sick is a rehearsal for greater days ahead, so don't run away from it — you'll learn to pray for the sick in the dry season and in the rainy season [2]. Fear is a spirit that keeps you from using your gifts, and the author describes fear as his greatest barrier to this ministry [4]. Keep your prayers short, as Jesus did — He prayed briefly for the sick, and short prayers are very powerful [3]. You can also pray with anointing oil, as James 5:14-15 and Mark 6:13 show, and believe that it is no longer ordinary oil but the healing anointing of the Holy Spirit [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *Am I Good For Nothing?*, chapter 2 of *The Preparation of the Gospel*, chapter 17 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*, chapter 15 of *Many Are Called* and chapter 20 of *Amplify Your Ministry with Miracles And Manifestations Of The Holy Spirit*.

Scriptures referenced: Mark 6:13; Mark 7:34-35; Luke 4:18; Luke 9:1-2; Luke 23:34; John 6:11; John 11:41-42; James 5:14-15.

items.question: How can I know my strengths and use them for God?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly. God has asked you to be strong in the grace He has given you, and whatever grace He has given you, you should flow in it [1]. Knowing your temperament — choleric, sanguine, melancholic or phlegmatic — will help you know your strengths and flow in them [1]. For example, if you are phlegmatic you have a grace to do the same thing repeatedly and to carry on in an unchanging environment, so be a good teacher, pastor or headmaster and flow in it [1]; if you are melancholic it is a grace from God to be talented, deep-thinking and faithful, so go ahead and flow in your strengths and in your God-given gift [1][2]; if you are choleric, recognize the grace to be a driving personality, a finisher of projects and a natural manager, and walk in that strength of leadership [2]; and if you are sanguine, the grace has been given to you to be cheerful, happy and pleasant at all times, so do not despise this great strength [2].

A true leader knows where his strength lies, and when you discover your strengths, flow in them and become a great leader [2][3]. Do not be a pastor because everyone is pastoring a church, and do not be a prophet because that is the latest fad in town [3]. Stay in the area which makes you unique, develop it and become strong [3]. And above all, make God your strength and trust in His mercy, for when you trust in other things you become weaker [4], as Psalm 52:6-8 says of the man who made not God his strength.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 27 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 6 of *The Determinants*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 52:6-8; Ecclesiastes 9:11; 2 Timothy 2:1; 2 Timothy 4:7.

items.question: How do I know my work for God is not a waste of time?
items.text:
What a good question to bring, and the books speak to it directly. Your labour in the Lord is not in vain: Solomon called his own work vanity, but Paul said his work was not in vain, "forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord" [2]. The work God gives you is itself a gift, and it is that work which energizes you [1].

You can also tell it is not wasted because doing the work helps you overcome your personal problems — as you minister the Word, those problems become smaller, and God has never used perfect people who have no problems [3]. items.question: How can I motivate the people who follow me as a leader?
items.text:
What a good question to be asking, pastor. The books speak to this directly.

First, be yourself and speak from your heart rather than reading a speech — people love to hear leaders speaking naturally from their hearts, and no one wants to follow a pretender [2]. Believe totally in the future your leadership is creating, and go yourself where you are trying to get people to follow you; you cannot get people to pray if you do not pray yourself [2][4]. The master key to leading people anywhere is to walk the road yourself — Jesus never told his disciples to do things he himself did not do [4].

Lead with the emotional nature of people in mind: a true leader inspires, and you cannot motivate people if you yourself are not motivated [3]. Speak to your people and raise their morale, for your failure to raise their morale is your failure to lead [8]. And make your followers love you rather than resent you: make them feel genuinely respected, transform them into eminent and distinguished men, and sacrifice to give them a future and a hope [1][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 79, 83, 91 and 92 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 9 of *A Good General*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 23:15-16; Matthew 26:35; Mark 1:17; Acts 3:6; Acts 20:33-37.

items.question: What does the Bible say happens to a society that stops being thankful to God?
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this. When people knew God but did not glorify Him or give thanks, they became vain in their imaginations and their foolish hearts were darkened, and professing themselves wise they became fools (Romans 1:21-22) [2][3]. Because of this unthankfulness, God gave them up — three times — to uncleanness, to vile affections, and to a debased mind, so that they exchanged the natural use of the woman and the man and burned in their lust one toward another (Romans 1:26-28) [1][3].

The books describe the result as a descent into total perversion, total foolishness, total madness and total destruction, and say the human race is teetering on the brink of destruction because of our ungratefulness [3]. They also say unthankfulness is listed among the terrible faults of the last days, when men will be more and more ungrateful (2 Timothy 3:1-5) [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *How Can I Say Thanks* and chapter 7 of *Pillars of Loyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Judges 9:16-21; Romans 1:21; Romans 1:26-28; Colossians 3:15; 1 Timothy 4:3-5; 2 Timothy 3:1-5.

items.question: How do I know if I've been called by God to do His work?
items.text:
What a good and weighty question. Our books say the call of God is not something you take to yourself: "no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is CALLED OF GOD, as was Aaron" (Hebrews 5:4) [6]. So the first mark to look for is a divine call rather than a human appointment, since the ministry is not a human institution [6].

One of the principal ways that call shows itself is a supernatural desire and interest in the work of the ministry [6]. Paul asked Timothy to look for the desire and didn't even mention the call, because the desire is a manifestation of a divine call [4]. That desire may not be a sensational experience, but it is a burden God puts there [6]. Alongside it comes a willing commitment, like Isaiah's "Here am I; send me" (Isaiah 6:8) [3], and a conviction that you are called, for without that conviction you cannot be a pastor [6].

You can also rest in this: your call is no accident. "Whom he did predestinate, them he also called" (Romans 8:30), so it is your destiny to be called, and those who believe they are called simply take God's Word, their dreams, and their quiet times more seriously [7]. If you already know God is calling you, do not refuse, for you could pay with your life for disobeying the divine call [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd* and chapter 2 of *Predestination*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 6:8; Romans 8:30; Romans 10:1; 1 Corinthians 9:16-17; 1 Timothy 4:15; Hebrews 5:4.

items.question: How do I forgive someone who hurt me very badly?
items.text:
I'm sorry for the hurt you're carrying. Our books speak to this.

Forgiveness means releasing the hurts, bitterness, and wickedness from your heart, giving up all claims against the one who offended you, cancelling any indebtedness, making no more mention of the matter, stopping resentment and anger, and cancelling all punishments you had planned [1]. It is a choice to let go and release the grudge, and it is possible for you to forgive — allow the Holy Spirit to help you [6].

One step that makes it easier is to analyse the offender: Jesus said of those killing Him, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34), and He made excuses for His own murderers — perhaps your offender is sick, ignorant, or confused [2][5]. Another step is to analyse your own past sins, "considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted" [5]. And remember you are equally in dire need of forgiveness from God, for if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you (Matthew 6:14) [3]. Walk in love and pray for your offenders [1].

Do not be afraid to forgive — your forgiveness is not the end of the story, for God says, "Vengeance is mine; I will repay" (Romans 12:19-20), and your duty is to forgive while God's duty is to repay [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 18 of *Those Who Are Offended*, chapters 5 and 8 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition* and chapter 59 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 147:3; Matthew 6:14; Luke 23:34; Romans 12:19-20; Ephesians 4:32; Hebrews 12:3.

items.question: A member has stopped coming to church and stopped praying. How do I help them come back to God?
items.text:
Our books speak to this. Staying in fellowship matters: if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship one with another (1 John 1:7), and if you are in the light you will go to church and fellowship with other Christians [3]. A Christian who doesn't pray is a Christian who will fall into one temptation after another until he eventually backslides, and Jesus told His disciples to pray because they might fall into temptation [8]. Also, anybody who does not want to be committed to a church will ultimately leave that church; an uncommitted Christian is a potential backslider [8].

So keep calling them home, and keep praying for them. It is time to come back home, and staying in fellowship is an important key to receiving the blessings of the Lord [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *How to Pray* and chapter 7 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 119:133; Proverbs 7:10; 1 John 1:7; 1 John 3:22.

items.question: What happens in my life when I don't pray?
items.text:
When you do not pray, your life is directed by happenstance—what looks like chance, luck, or fate is often governed by natural and spiritual forces you cannot see [1]. Ahab's death, which looked like a random arrow, was actually orchestrated by evil spirits [2]. Without prayer, your life follows the stereotyped patterns set by the major curses in this world—the curse on Adam, on Eve, and on Ham [2][4].

You also leave your life open to the decisions of other people. As Pilate's decision shows, human beings are constantly making choices that affect you, and if you do not pray, the will of capricious and unreasonable men will be implemented in your life [3]. And when you do not pray, you do not intervene in the spirit realm, where spiritual events trigger things in the natural world [5]. The whole world lies in wickedness, and without prayer your life is governed by the wickedness of men [6] and by Satan, who is called the god of this world (2 Corinthians 4:4) and who directs its wars, conflicts, and sorrows [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How to Pray* and chapter 2 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 22:30-35; Proverbs 3:13-16; 2 Corinthians 4:4; 1 John 5:19; Revelation 6:1-8.

items.question: How can a young person stay away from sexual sin?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and I'm glad you asked. First, respect your sexuality rather than denying it — a proper respect for youthful lusts, rather than a denial of them, will save you from them [3]. The will of God is clear that you abstain from sexual immorality (1 Thessalonians 4:3-4), so make it one of your clearest and most energetic goals to live a sexually pure life, and stay away from anyone who would want such a relationship with you [2]. Each person keeps himself from fornication differently, so find out what God's will is for your own journey — it may be never reading certain books or watching certain films, never having certain friends, or not working with women or having female secretaries [2].

Practically, the books say very young people should not enter into relationships for courtship, for there is a time for everything (Ecclesiastes 3:1), and you should only enter relationships that lead to marriage [5]. Also, don't hide — sit in the front, be visible, and make sure your pastor knows your name, for those who sit far away are often practicing some kind of evil [8]. And take heart: holiness is engineered by the Spirit of holiness, not by being older, and every young person can be empowered by that Spirit (Romans 1:4) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*, chapters 10, 13 and 24 of *Ready@20* and chapter 4 of *Spiritual Dangers*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 3:16; Ecclesiastes 3:1; Jeremiah 2:5; Luke 15:13; Luke 15:30; John 8:46; Romans 1:4; Ephesians 5:5-6; 1 Thessalonians 4:3-4; James 4:8.

items.question: How do I know if I'm ready to step into a bigger role in ministry?
items.text:
Friend, the books give you some honest questions to sit with rather than a quick formula. They ask whether you are ready to leave familiar things behind, even old friends and acquaintances, as Abram was told to go forth from his relatives (Genesis 12:1) [1], and whether you are ready to leave your own country, region, or neighbourhood, since God's command is to go to the uttermost parts of the earth [1]. They also ask whether you can bring your whole family along this road, since some spouses reject the uncertainty of it all, and a wise man will not marry someone allergic to uncertainty (Genesis 18:19) [8].

The books also warn that readiness is proven over time, not assumed. God does not put inexperienced people into the ministry, and Scripture says a leader must not be a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil (1 Timothy 3:6) [4]. There are levels in God's service — doing the work, having a gift, having a ministry, and occupying an office — and you prove yourself before being put into an office (2 Timothy 4:5; Romans 12:6; Romans 11:13) [4]. One book even says many are frustrated because they entered full-time ministry too quickly, and that entering even a year early can change the results [3].

So the counsel here is to ask these questions honestly in your heart and settle them, and to let your readiness be shown by faithful service and experience rather than by eagerness alone [1][3][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)*, chapter 14 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd* and chapter 15 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 12:1; Genesis 18:19; Romans 11:13; Romans 12:6; 1 Corinthians 1:24; 1 Timothy 3:6; 2 Timothy 4:5.

items.question: Why is the shepherd's ministry so important in the church?
items.text:
The shepherd's ministry matters because it is the shepherd, not the prophet, whose absence scatters the sheep; God promises to set up shepherds who will save His people, and it is through the shepherd that the earth yields her increase and the people dwell safely [1]. The prophet Ezekiel declares this, and the ministry of the shepherd is prophetically destined to change the landscape of the church [1].

It is also a principal duty of the shepherd to feed the sheep, and the authority to lead is given to those with the ability to feed [2]. Jesus said to Peter three times, "Feed my sheep" (John 21:17), showing how important it is to the Lord that His sheep are well fed on the Word of God [2]. Alongside this, one of the principal ministries of a shepherd is to comfort the sheep, so that every sheep can say, "Your rod and your staff comfort me" (Psalm 23:4) [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church* and chapter 11 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 23:4; Proverbs 22:10; Micah 7:14; Mark 6:46; Luke 5:15-16; John 21:17.

items.question: How can I show God that I'm thankful for everything He's done for me?
items.text:
What a good question to ask, pastor. The books say the only real way to say "thank you" to Jesus is with your life — not just with songs or words you've learned, but with something genuine that comes from you [5]. One way is to give Him your reasonable service, presenting your body as a living sacrifice, which is your reasonable service, as Romans 12:1 says [2][4]. Another is to labour more abundantly than everyone else, working harder than all others, as Paul said in 1 Corinthians 15:10, because you're conscious of the grace shown to you [2].

The books also say to thank God in everything, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you (1 Thessalonians 5:18), and to give thanks always for all things to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ (Ephesians 5:20) — thank Him for the good, the bad, and the ugly [6]. And giving thanks is a mighty key to working great miracles; perhaps you'll see the greatest miracles of your life when you stand before an impossible situation and give thanks to God [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1 and 4 of *How Can I Say Thanks*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 107:1; Romans 12:1-2; 1 Corinthians 15:10; Ephesians 5:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:18; 2 Timothy 3:2.

items.question: Where do demons come from?
items.text:
The books say demons are not the same as fallen angels or Satan; they are a separate kind of creature, called *diamonion* in the Greek, while the devil comes from *diabolos* [1][2]. Their origin is traced to the fallen angels who left heaven and had sexual relations with women, producing giants and hybrid "para-human" offspring; when those abnormal beings died, their half-human, half-angel spirits could not go to heaven or hell, so they were confined to the earth and roam about as demons [1][2]. As Enoch 15:8-10 puts it, "the giants, who are produced from the spirits and flesh, shall be called evil spirits on the earth" [2].

The books also describe another kind of unclean spirit: fallen angels also sinned against birds, animals, fish and reptiles, and the offspring of those unions continued to interbreed, producing the wicked spirit-animal creatures known as "unclean (animal) spirits" [4]. And these spirits, we're told, "afflict, oppress, destroy, attack, war, destroy, and cause trouble on the earth" [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 15 and 17 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies*.

Scriptures referenced: Jude 6.

items.question: How can I become a friend of God like Abraham was?
items.text:
What a good thing to long for. Our books say that Abraham was called a friend of God, and they show how he came to be one.

He became God's friend by being willing to sacrifice his only son, and this was the test of obedience, which is the test of love [3][4]. He obeyed God even to the point of sacrificing his own son, and there was no third party between Abraham and God—no adviser, no friend lurking in the shadows to influence him after he had met with God [2]. He was completely sold out to God; there was nothing he would not do for the Lord [2].

The books also say that every Christian will have an "Isaac" that God will ask for one day, and you can only give up your "Isaac" if you are fully surrendered to God [5]. So do not let anything become too precious to you, for anything that becomes too precious will attract the attention of the Lord and He may ask for it; God wants to be the only God in your life [5]. Before God can bless you in a special way, He needs to be sure about you, so don't hold back anything from the Lord [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 11 of *If You Love The Lord*, chapter 12 of *One Thousand Micro Churches* and chapter 5 of *The Art of Following*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 22:16-17; Deuteronomy 13:1-3; Isaiah 41:8; Daniel 8:11-13; John 12:24; Romans 12:1-2; 2 Corinthians 8:24; James 2:23; 1 John 5:21.

items.question: How should I keep the Sabbath day as a Christian?
items.text:
Friend, our books speak to this plainly. The Sabbath is a day for going to church and hearing the word of God — Jesus went to the synagogue on the Sabbath as His custom, and Paul and Barnabas went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day [1][7]. It is God-time, not family time, and not a day for football, golf, washing, or visiting friends [1][6]. It is also a day of rest: "Faith loves rest," and not keeping the Sabbath and not resting is a manifestation of faithlessness, for "he that believeth shall not make haste" [4]. The Sabbath is a sign between God and His people, a holy day, and keeping it sets you apart as peculiar and obedient [3][8].

One caution: the books do not agree on which day. One says the Sabbath is a day of rest "whether Saturday, Sunday or Monday," and that you should not worry about which day of the week it is, only that you have chosen a day to set apart for God [7]. Another speaks of the Sabbath as the seventh day and of Jews observing it on Saturday [3][8]. Both views are presented; I leave the choosing to you and the Holy Spirit [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Seven Great Principles*, chapter 25 of *Stir It Up*, chapter 72 of *Faith Secrets* and chapter 4 of *WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 16:23; Exodus 31:12-17; Exodus 35:2; Leviticus 23:27-32; Ezekiel 20:21; Malachi 3:10; Matthew 12:12; Mark 1:21; Luke 14:3; Acts 13:14-16 and 2 more.

items.question: How can I have a closer relationship with God?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and the heart of it is drawing near to Him personally. "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you" (James 4:8), and the way you do that is not in public — not at church services, conventions, or crusades — but through a regular daily quiet time, where you know Him personally rather than just knowing about Him [1][3][5][7]. It is up to you to draw near to Him on a daily basis, rather than waiting for Him to come to you [3][7].

When you are alone with someone, you become close and intimate, you develop a bond not easily acquired in public, you acquire knowledge you cannot acquire in public, and you can receive a private impartation — so being alone with God is where that closeness grows [8]. One caution the books give: as you get closer to God you may sense your own unworthiness and sin, and to love Him properly you must overcome that inferiority by accepting that you are forgiven and that the past is washed away by the blood of Jesus [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapter 6 of *Attempt Great Things for God*, chapter 5 of *The Secret* and chapter 21 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 27:33-36; Ephesians 4:3; Philippians 3:10; James 4:8; 1 John 1:1-2.

items.question: How can a husband and wife make love in a way that is enjoyable for both of them?
items.text:
What a good thing to want for each other. Your books say sex was created by God as something beautiful and pleasurable to be enjoyed by both husband and wife, not just for procreation [1], and that it is an art to be learned and developed, about having fun with your partner and showing care rather than scoring 10 out of 10 for performance [5].

So decide together to make it pleasurable, with both of you setting out to give and derive maximum excitement [1]. Be nice to each other during the day with small thoughtful acts, look nice, smell nice and be clean, and choose a nice place and lighting that suits you [1]. Let foreplay begin with endearing conversation, loving pats, hugs and kisses [1], and keep stimulating each other during the act by holding tightly, caressing and kissing [4]. Talk to each other and express your feelings during the act, and let your partner know which movements stimulate you or distract you [1][4]. Remember that a woman's arousal builds slowly, like an electric iron heating up, while a man's is like a light switched on [1][4], so the husband should continue kissing and caressing her until she is sexually excited [1]. Kissing is an important form of intimacy, encouraged in marriage, and kissing whilst making love is exciting (Song of Solomon 1:2) [3]. You must also satisfy each other at all times, and make a conscious effort to admire each other's body and beauty (Proverbs 5:19) [3]. Finally, let your partner feel that he or she has done something wonderful to you [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 28, 31 and 38 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 5:19; Song of Songs 1:2.

items.question: How can I pray like Jesus did?
items.text:
What a good thing to want, pastor. Our books hold up Jesus' own prayer life as the pattern.

There are times to pray short and powerful prayers, as Jesus did at Lazarus' tomb, believing God has heard you and then acting boldly [1][5]. But there are also times to spend long hours in prayer, as Jesus did when He continued all night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12) and rose a great while before day to pray in a solitary place (Mark 1:35) [1][5]. You can pray on the same topic for hours; it is not useless repetition, it is praying like Jesus did [1][2][3]. Start with one hour and graduate to three, then five and seven hours [1][5].

Jesus also prayed with strong crying and tears, as Hebrews 5:7 says, and so can you, though you need not always shout [2][3]. And He gave thanks: "In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you" (1 Thessalonians 5:18) [2][3]. One more thing from the books: pray to your heavenly Father and not to anyone else, as Jesus directed in John 16:23 [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 6 of *100% Answered Prayer* and chapter 7 of *How to Pray*.

Scriptures referenced: Mark 1:35; Luke 1:38; Luke 6:12; John 11:41-42; John 16:23; 1 Thessalonians 5:18; Hebrews 5:7.

items.question: How can my wife and I build a strong marriage?
items.text:
What a good thing to want. The books say a happy home does not just happen; it must be developed, and nothing happens by chance [7]. So start with Christ acknowledged as the foundation and head of the home, for the one who hears His sayings and does them is like a man who laid his foundation on a rock, as Luke 6:47-48 says [7]. When God is the focus of both of you, you draw closer to each other because your closeness to God draws you together [7].

Build your marriage around the church, and let the Word of God be your manual for marriage [2]. Hold regular quiet times together, or each of you regularly when that is not possible, but by all means find time once in a while to do it together, especially with the children; attend church services and be involved, sitting together in church [3]. Think as a Christian spouse: do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit, but in humility consider others better than yourselves, as Philippians 2:3 says, reconciling the plans you each held before marriage to suit the home, willing to give up certain interests for its sake, and ready to compromise rather than always insisting on your own way [3]. And be the best of friends, sharing every success, disappointment, joy and pain together, speaking the truth in love to one another, as Ephesians 4:15 says [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 7 and 9 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Job 32:17-20; Psalms 1:1-6; Proverbs 14:4; Proverbs 18:21; Proverbs 24:3; Luke 6:47-48; Ephesians 4:15; Philippians 2:3.

items.question: What does it mean if God rewards my faithfulness with more work instead of rest?
items.book: WOM15. The Reward for Hard Work is More Work
items.text:
It means God is treating your faithfulness as a qualification for greater trust. The reward for being faithful with small things is to be given bigger things to work on [5], and the reward for working well with what belongs to another is to be given your own [1]. So more work is not a punishment but a sign of God's gratitude for your efforts and a credential for future ministry [1][3].

The books do hold out rest as a reward too — "they may rest from their labours" (Revelation 14:12-13) [2] — but they also say plainly that God does not only give rest, He gives more work after the period of rest [2]. So do not expect holidays and restful seasons; expect more hard work [4], and keep pressing on rather than thinking of retiring [3][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 5 and 8 of *WOM15. The Reward for Hard Work is More Work*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 16:27; Luke 16:10-12; 1 Timothy 5:17-18; Hebrews 11:6.

items.question: How can I grow and be more successful without becoming overconfident and setting myself up for a fall?
items.text:
What a good and sober question. The books speak directly to it.

Growth and success are real gifts, but the danger is that pride grows alongside them. Overconfidence is one of the marks of the pride of a novice, and at its end stage every sin gets complicated by pride [1]. If you regard yourself or your position in Christ as foolproof, you are in danger of backsliding — especially if you have had promotion in church or have been used by God in the past [2]. Where you are over-confident is where you can be the weakest, because you have dropped your guard [2].

The safeguard the books hold out is humility, which keeps you learning. Ministers of the gospel stop learning at the rate at which they become proud, unable to receive from people they despise, and so they stop growing in the Lord and in the ministry [3]. When you are humble like a child, you copy things easily; when you lose that humility, you do not want to copy, even if it is a good thing [3]. Staying on the right track is largely by the grace of God, and not by your own strength [2]. And be careful how you speak of others' weaknesses — you can tell a Christian is over-confident by the way he talks about the weaknesses of others, criticizing them as though he could never make the same mistakes [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Not A Novice*, chapter 5 of *Backsliding* and chapter 2 of *Those who are Proud*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 16:1-4; 1 Corinthians 10:12.
