items.question: How can I know the real number of people attending our church instead of just guessing?
items.text:
What you're describing is exactly what the books call Type 1 Counting — the number of people physically present, counting actual heads rather than estimating [1][4]. The author says he prefers to stay with Type 1 Counting "because there can be no variation in the method of counting heads who are actually present" [8], and he calls the Sunday morning attendance the best number to use for monitoring progress in a general way [4].

He also warns against the guessing you want to avoid: Type 5 is rough estimates based on experience, which can be quite accurate or totally misleading [1], and Type 6 is "wild and unreasonable guessing" [1]. He urges pastors to stop making wild guesses about the number of people in their churches, because when you know the actual number of souls you are ministering to, you will be motivated to work harder [2]. He even says that when he asked his data officer for the figure and heard it, he was depressed for a week — but that if you cannot tell yourself the truth, you cannot be a good leader [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 45 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Luke 13:23; John 8:32.

items.question: There is a woman in our church who manipulates and controls people. How do I deal with her?
items.book: Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order
items.text:
Our books speak directly to this. A Jezebel must not be allowed to operate freely in the church, and it angers God when she is left unchecked [7]. It takes the collective rebuke of church leadership to deal with a Jezebel; one person crying foul will not correct or control her [3]. God wants more people to identify the Jezebels in our midst and stop them [3].

Many pastors are too dignified or want to keep good relations with everybody, so they will not rebuke and correct wives who are out of order [7]. But if a Jezebel is allowed to go uncorrected, you may lose everything, just as Elijah lost his ministry [7]. One man described the greatest mistake of his life as failing to confront the Jezebel in their senior pastor's marriage; they said they should have been her enemy and fought openly no matter the cost, and because they did not, it cost them everything [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 4 and 21 of *Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order* and chapter 15 of *Can’t You Do
Just a Little Bit More?*.

Scriptures referenced: Revelation 2:20.

items.question: What will heaven and the new earth be like?
items.book: Who Is He That Overcometh the World
items.text:
What a hope we have, pastor. The books say we are expecting to arrive in another world very soon, and that everything we have gathered and built on this earth will be left behind [2]. The world we know will be replaced by the world that is to come [2], and in that world God Himself will dwell with us — His presence will be with us everywhere, and He will wipe away all tears from our eyes [1].

There will be no more death, sorrow, crying, or pain, for the former things will have passed away [1][3], and there shall be no more curse [3][4]. There will be no sea or oceans there [1][2], and the New Jerusalem will be a very beautiful city with a river of life and a tree of life whose leaves are for the healing of the nations [4][5]. No evil thing, no abomination, and no liar can enter it, and there will be no night and no need of sun or candle [4]. The kingdoms of this world will become the kingdoms of our Lord and of His Christ, and He shall reign for ever and ever (Revelation 11:15) [5]. People we know as nobodies on earth will become rulers of that world [5]. Truly, this world is not our home [1].

items.question: How can churches grow in poor areas if they can't afford to pay pastors and workers?
items.book: Laikos Lay People and the Ministry
items.text:
The books speak directly to this. The key is the lay or tent ministry—pastors and evangelists who labour without being paid, as Paul did when he worked as a tent maker alongside Aquila and Priscilla [1][2]. Most of the ripened harvest fields are in the poor regions of the world, and the ministry of unpaid pastors and evangelists is the key to continued church planting there [1][2].

So the counsel is practical: find a job and start or pastor the church as a lay person, rather than becoming financially dependent on a small congregation [5][6]. When people see you are not ministering for financial gain, they will be more interested in your new church [5][6]. And remember that many kinds of workers—doctors, teachers, accountants, lawyers, and more—can serve as fruitful lay pastors who are not paid by the church [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry*, chapters 9 and 20 of *Church Planting*, chapter 7 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 3 of *Church Growth*.

items.question: What does it mean to be called by God?
items.text:
Being called by God is a great privilege and honour — to be summoned distinctly, identified and called out by name and selected by God [1]. In the Hebrew, *qara* means to call out, to address by name, even to make someone famous; in Greek, *kletos* means to be invited or appointed [1]. Moses, Bezaleel, Samuel, Zacchaeus and many of the disciples were called out by name [1].

It also means you have been separated for His purposes — detached from the larger group and withdrawn from secular life and ideals, even from family and friends [2]. The Hebrew *badal* means to distinguish and make a difference between you and others, and the Greek *aphorizo* means to keep apart by a boundary [2]. You have received an office with special responsibilities and authority [3], a gift — a natural capacity freely given, so that called people seem to do certain things effortlessly [4] — and special mercy, God's kindness and pity shown to your pitiful state [5]. You are appointed for a special purpose [5], sent out properly, for God dispatches you to fetch many souls from the grip of the devil [7], and you have received a ministry, a particular line of Kingdom work [8]. And your calling is according to His own purpose and grace, given us in Christ Jesus before the world began, as 2 Timothy 1:9 says — so it is important not only to obey the call but to find out the purpose for which God called you [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Many Are Called* and chapter 1 of *Predestination*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 29:1; Deuteronomy 10:8; Deuteronomy 32:8; 1 Chronicles 15:16-19; 1 Chronicles 23:13; Mark 1:19-20; Luke 2:40; John 1:14; Acts 13:2; Romans 1:1 and 10 more.

items.question: What should someone who just gave their life to Christ learn first?
items.text:
What a joy to hear of someone newly born again. The first thing is to understand what has actually happened to them: if you are born again, you have had a spiritual heart transplant, and you need understanding of the concept of salvation so you can grow in grace [7]. Wisdom is the principal thing, and you gain understanding when you know principles [7].

They also need to be taught the elementary principles of the oracles of God, because the way a person is taught those fundamentals permanently determines their spiritual make-up [2]. And they should be pointed to the one who led them to Christ, for that person is someone never to be forgotten — as 1 Corinthians 4:15 says, "in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Those Who Forget* and chapter 1 of *Seven Great Principles*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 21:34-36; 1 Corinthians 4:15; Hebrews 5:12.

items.question: Why is it dangerous to think you're untouchable or indispensable in ministry?
items.text:
Thinking you are untouchable is a dangerous attitude, because it is really pride and deception. As Absalom felt he could not be sacked or transferred, so anyone who feels indispensable has developed the wrong attitude, and pride always comes before a fall [1][3]. The book warns that as soon as you begin to think of yourself as indispensable, your delusions will lead to your destruction [1].

It is also dangerous because God is not bound to keep using you as you are. Do not think that you are indispensable; if you do not do what God wants you to do, your ministry will be taken away from you and given to another, as Luke 19:24 says, "Take from him the pound, and give it to him that hath ten pounds" [2]. And a person who feels indispensable is simply dangerous to have around [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Those who are Dangerous Sons* and chapter 6 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 14:32; Luke 19:24; Romans 11:29.

items.question: What happens when you pray for wisdom?
items.book: Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry
items.text:
When you pray for wisdom, God gives it generously to those who ask — as James 1:5 says, if any of you lacks wisdom, ask of God, who gives liberally and does not upbraid [6]. Solomon is the great example: he asked for an understanding heart to judge God's people, and the request pleased the Lord [6].

The books describe several effects. Praying for wisdom gives you a large heart — a great depth of understanding and insight [5]. It makes your wisdom exceed the wisdom prevailing in your nation, as Solomon's wisdom excelled all the wisdom of the East and of Egypt (1 Kings 4:30) [1][5]. It makes you wiser than your contemporaries, as Solomon was wiser than all men (1 Kings 4:31) [1]. It makes you a man of proverbs and songs (1 Kings 4:32) [1], and it makes you appreciate nature — trees, beasts, fowl, creeping things, and fishes (1 Kings 4:33) [2]. It also causes people to travel from afar to hear the wisdom God has given you, and even kings and great men to pay attention to it (1 Kings 4:34), for by wisdom kings reign (Proverbs 8:15) [3].

Beyond that, wisdom makes curses more bearable and overrules their effect — when you get wisdom, riches, honour, and length of days arrive in your life (Proverbs 3:13-16) [4]. Women are helped by wisdom, delivered from blindly following men, and through wisdom, which is medical science, childbearing is not as destructive [4][8]. And the black man who has historically been at the bottom rises through the gift of wisdom, no longer the lowest and least when he walks in the wisdom of God [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 26 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry* and chapter 3 of *How to Pray*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 3:9-11; 1 Kings 4:29-34; Proverbs 3:13-16; Proverbs 8:15; Luke 11:13; 2 Corinthians 4:4; James 1:5.

items.question: How can I avoid becoming too familiar with my leaders or with people I look up to?
items.book: Those Who Pretend, Intimidate And Are Familiar
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and the heart of it is guarding your respect and awe for those you look up to. Familiarity means knowing someone so well that you lose your admiration, respect, and sense of awe, becoming presumptuous [6]. So be quick to detect the subtle signs of it, as Jesus was quick to notice when Peter was out of order [3]. Peter's friendship with Jesus exposed his familiarity, and he stepped out of line by rebuking and instructing the Lord [5]. When that happened, Jesus addressed and confronted it urgently, cutting Peter down to size [8].

Practically, the books warn that certain situations make familiarity more likely: frequent interaction with the leader, knowing too much about his private life, being his friend, and being promoted [4]. So maintain a degree of mystique, since the less people know about your private realities, the more they can receive from you [4]. It also helps to keep clear distinctions between ranks, as Jesus sat on the donkey while the disciples walked [1][7], and to avoid monotony, since repetitiveness and dullness are the perfect contexts for familiarity [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 8 and 10 of *Those Who Pretend, Intimidate And Are Familiar*, chapter 95 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 13 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 41:9; Matthew 16:15-17; Matthew 16:22-23; Mark 1:37-39; Mark 6:1-6.

items.question: What does the anointing do for someone's ministry?
items.text:
The anointing brings supernatural help for your life and ministry, as David said, "I have given help to one who is mighty" (Psalm 89:19b) [1]. It raises you up to heights in ministry and establishes you — "I have found David My servant; With My holy oil I have anointed him. With whom My hand will be established" (Psalm 89:20-21) [1]. It introduces strength to your ministry, so that "My arm also will strengthen him" (Psalm 89:21) [1], and it protects you from deception, the blindness and hypocrisy Jesus rebuked when He said, "You blind guides, who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel!" (Matthew 23:24) [1].

It also enables you to build and restore, laying brick upon brick and making something out of shattered lives [2], and it causes people who are bound to be set free, for logical teaching cannot open prison doors [4]. It comforts those who mourn (Isaiah 61:2) [4], restores your beauty and attractiveness (Isaiah 61:3) [4], reaches beyond your own country and tribe (Isaiah 61:5) [2], and gives you a long-lasting ministry, for "His seed shall endure forever" (Psalm 89:36-37) [6]. It even affects your children, as God said, "So I will establish his descendants forever" (Psalm 89:29) [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 15 of *Steps to the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 89:19-21; Psalms 89:29; Psalms 89:36-37; Isaiah 61:2-3; Isaiah 61:5-6; Matthew 23:24.

items.question: What does the Bible say about the importance of skill for getting things built?
items.text:
Yes, friend, the books speak to this plainly. Skill is the master key to building, and failure to build reveals a lack of practical skills — impractical men build nothing [1][2]. Skill is what determines whether you will build a house at all [1].

It also determines who is chosen and how far you rise: Daniel and his friends were elevated and found ten times better than all the magicians because God gave them knowledge and skill, as Daniel 1:17-20 records [2]. And skill is not something you are simply born with — it is determined by humility and a determination to learn something new, as Solomon showed when he acknowledged that none among them could skill to hew timber like the Sidonians (1 Kings 5) [1].

One caution from the books: it is not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, saith the Lord of hosts (Zechariah 4:6) — the Church will be built by the power of the Holy Spirit, not by education or human ability alone [6]. So skill matters greatly, but it is God's power that ultimately builds His house, for except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it (Psalm 127:1) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 15 of *The Determinants*, chapter 64 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 3 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Chronicles 28:10; 1 Chronicles 28:20; 2 Chronicles 2:7-8; Psalms 127:1; Ecclesiastes 9:11; Daniel 1:17-20; Zechariah 4:6; Luke 7:4-5.

items.question: How should a Christian live simply and avoid wasting money?
items.text:
The books speak to this plainly. Wasting what God has put in your hand costs you your position and your prosperity: the steward who wasted was told to give an account, "for thou mayest be no longer steward" (Luke 16:1-2), and the prodigal "wasted his substance with riotous living" until he began to be in want (Luke 15:12-14) [1]. So cut out waste — most poor nations waste half their resources, and that is why they stay poor [6] — and do not have an expensive lifestyle; cut your coat according to your size and avoid grandiose things others are doing [6].

Watch the company you keep, for the prodigal did not waste his money alone — there were harlots to help him, and "evil company corrupts good habits" (1 Corinthians 15:33) [3]. Be wary of get-rich-quick schemes; the Kingdom is like a mustard seed that needs time to grow, and there are no short cuts [4]. And be careful of lust for things apart from God's Word, for "the lusts of other things entering in, choke the word" (Mark 4:19) — kill those desires while they are small [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 10 of *Opportunities*, chapters 3 and 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 2 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 30:3-6; Psalms 27:4; Mark 4:19; Luke 15:12-14; Luke 15:25; Luke 16:1-2; 1 Corinthians 15:33.

items.question: How did Paul become equal to or greater than Peter as an apostle?
items.text:
The books say Paul rose to the level of Peter, the chiefest apostle, because the grace of revelation visited Paul rather than Peter, and Paul laboured more abundantly than all the apostles, saying "I laboured more abundantly than they all, yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me" (1 Corinthians 15:10) [1][2]. Paul himself said he was "not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles" (2 Corinthians 11:5) [1][3].

They also describe this as wisdom: Paul caught up with those ahead of him through "the catching-up wisdom," which Peter acknowledged as "the wisdom given unto him" (2 Peter 3:14-16), and that wisdom had two parts — walking in the grace of God and working harder than those ahead of you [6]. Another passage says promotion in ministry comes through an abundance of revelations, and that Paul was a man of books, reading and quoting abundantly from them [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *BEMA Judgment And Justice*, chapter 13 of *JUDAS
Who is he??*, chapter 7 of *WOM13. The Big Secret - Your Ministry Depends on Books* and chapter 13 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*.

items.question: What does it mean to make a C-turn toward Jesus instead of a U-turn away from him?
items.book: What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent
items.text:
A C-turn is a swerve to the side — not a reversal, but a manoeuvre that takes you off the wrong course onto a better way [2][3]. Andrew and John show this: they had been disciples of John the Baptist, and when John pointed out the Lamb of God they knew it was time to move on; they did not make a U-turn away from the ministry, but a C-turn that took them deeper and further into God and brought them closer to Jesus [1]. Peter is another example — the fisherman became the apostle because he was capable of swerving off the layman's road and into full-time ministry, leaving his nets immediately when Jesus said, "Follow Me, and I will make you fishers of men" (Matthew 4:18-20) [3].

Jesus Himself made a C-turn, moving away from the country of the Gadarenes when the people asked Him to leave (Luke 8:37); He did not stop His ministry of casting out devils and healing people, He just shifted to where He was more welcome [2][3]. So it is not wisdom to be too stiff or insistent on your original plan — that can get you into big trouble; you must be flexible and capable of C-turns [3].

A U-turn is different: it is a reversal of your former decisions, a manoeuvre in which you go back on decisions you made earlier, and if you are not capable of U-turns you are not capable of repenting from your mistakes [4]. The prodigal son gives the best example — he arose and went to his father, reversing all his former decisions and humbly returning to his proper place (Luke 15:18-20) [4]. Zacchaeus made a U-turn when he met Jesus, turning away from corruption and swindling (Luke 19:8), and a U-turn is true repentance [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 4:18-20; Luke 8:37; Luke 15:18-20; Luke 19:8; John 1:35-37.

items.question: What does it mean to be a person of faith?
items.text:
Being a person of faith means walking in obedience to God — faith is equated with obedience, so an obedient person is a man of faith, and obeying God is the exercising of your faith [1]. It also means having a good attitude toward God and His Word, since your attitude reveals your faith, and faith comes by hearing the preaching of the Word [2]. And it means persisting in prayer even when there seems to be no response, for anyone who persists in prayer is a man of faith [3].

Faith is the assurance of things hoped for and the conviction of things not seen (Hebrews 11:1), and God has dealt to every man a measure of faith (Romans 12:3), so everyone has some amount of it to develop [5]. It also means being willing to walk in risk and uncertainty and to move forward rather than sit in doubt and unbelief [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 5 and 10 of *Faith Secrets*, chapter 5 of *Pr 6. Prayer Opportunities* and chapter 2 of *Name It Claim It Take It*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 9:22-23; Romans 12:3; Hebrews 11:1.

items.question: How do I become anointed by the Holy Spirit?
items.text:
Friend, our books say plainly that the anointing is the Holy Spirit Himself, and that God decides who becomes anointed — He hides Himself and is not easily found, so you must ask, seek, and knock [8]. Alongside that sovereign choice, they describe steps: being led by the Holy Spirit, even when He leads you against your natural inclinations [1][4]; waiting on God, as the disciples waited in Jerusalem and as Isaiah 40:31 promises new strength to those who wait on the Lord [2]; and living in love and unity, for the Spirit fell at Pentecost when they were all with one accord in one place (Acts 2:1) [2].

They also speak of receiving the Spirit by the hearing of faith — soaking in messages on the anointing until you are saturated, as one man listened to Kenneth Hagin for ten years before he received the anointing to teach [3]. And they say to flow with the Holy Spirit as a real person, talking with Him and recognizing His gentle pressures and sudden gusts, as the wind of Acts 2:2 [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 5 and 8 of *Steps to the Anointing*, chapter 13 of *Seeing And Hearing* and chapter 1 of *Flow in the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 28:1; Isaiah 40:31; Isaiah 45:15; Matthew 4:1; Luke 4:1-15; John 20:22; Acts 1:4; Acts 2:1-2.

items.question: Different topic: how do I pray effectively?
items.text:
Our books have plenty to say on that. Pray strategic Bible prayers, letting your prayers be guided by the Word of God — for instance Ephesians 1:17-19 and Ephesians 3:15-19 are powerful prayers a minister should pray [1]. Pray fervently, ardently and with passion, for the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much (James 5:16) [1][2]. Pray in tongues, as Paul did when he said, "I thank God that I speak in tongues more than you all" (1 Corinthians 14:18) [2]. And have discussions with the Holy Spirit, hearing His voice as well, since the Comforter will teach you all things (John 14:26) [2].

You can also pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17), keeping in touch with God on the bus, in the office, or in the shower [3]. For prayer to be effective it must be habitual, and it is important to enter your closet and pray for long periods, as Jesus did when He continued all night in prayer (Luke 6:12) [3][5]. Develop the ability to pray four times a day — morning, afternoon, evening and all-the-time — for morning prayer meets God before you meet the devil (Mark 1:35) [5]. There are also short, powerful prayers for crisis moments, as Jesus prayed at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:41-42), and long prayers for hours, as He prayed for the will of God to be done [7][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Transform Your Pastoral Ministry*, chapters 1 and 7 of *How to Pray* and chapter 2 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*.

items.question: How do I know God will take me back after I've turned away from him?
items.text:
Our books speak to this. God promises mercy and forgiveness to those who love Him: "God promises to forgive and forget the sins of those who love him," and He keeps covenant and mercy with them that love Him, as Deuteronomy 7:9-10 says [8]. So if you love the Lord, He will keep His covenant with you — no love, no covenant [8].

One passage also tells of a man who laughed at others' worship and feared he had committed the unpardonable sin, but an older Christian explained that he had not sinned against the Holy Ghost and could still be forgiven [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Lord I Know You Need Somebody* and chapter 12 of *If You Love The Lord*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 7:9-10.

items.question: How can I grow spiritually and bear fruit as a Christian?
items.text:
What a good thing to long for. Our books say plainly that every Christian should aim to be fruitful, because Christ saved us so that we would go and bear fruit, as John 15:16 says [5]. And they tell us that if you don't go forward, you will go backwards, so it matters that you have spiritual goals and press toward the mark, as Philippians 3:13, 14 puts it [5].

Several obstacles are named. You must overcome spiritual sickness — laziness, pride, living in sin, or habits that keep you from even sharing the Gospel — since 2 Peter 1:5-8 says these things make you neither barren nor unfruitful [2]. You must overcome immaturity, growing from childhood to adulthood, not tossed about by every wind of doctrine [1]. You must overcome instability by abiding in Christ, for as John 15:4, 5 says, the branch cannot bear fruit of itself except it abide [4]. And you must overcome inactivity: witnessing, teaching, and helping in the church will all help you get active in the things of God [3].

One book also says that when you are spiritually mature you are dominated by the Spirit, and the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance, as Galatians 5:22-25 lists [6]. So abide, be planted, and stay long enough to be watered and tended [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *Many Are Called*, chapter 9 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 6 of *Seven Great Principles*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 92:13-14; John 15:4-5; John 15:16; 1 Corinthians 13:11; Galatians 5:22-25; Philippians 3:13-14; Colossians 1:10; 2 Peter 1:5-8.

items.question: How can a young person deal with sexual desires and stay pure?
items.text:
What a good and honest question. The books speak to this directly, and they begin by telling you to respect your sexuality rather than deny it — desires are real forces, and a proper respect for youthful lusts, rather than a denial of them, will save you from them [4]. They are also clear that these cravings are peculiar to the young; Ecclesiastes 12:5 says "desire shall fail" in old age, so this is your chance to be an example in purity, as 1 Timothy 4:12 says [1][5].

The command is to flee: "Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart" (2 Timothy 2:22) [2][5]. And the will of God is plain — 1 Thessalonians 4:3-4 says this is your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality — so you must find out your own way of staying away from fornication, whether that means avoiding certain books or films, certain friends, or certain places [6]. You are not left to do this alone: holiness is engineered by the Spirit of holiness, not by age, and every young person can be empowered by Him to live free from sin [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 10, 12, 13 and 20 of *Ready@20* and chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 3:16; Genesis 41:46; Ecclesiastes 12:5; John 8:46; Romans 1:4; Ephesians 5:5-6; 1 Thessalonians 4:3-4; 1 Timothy 4:12; 2 Timothy 2:22; Revelation 14:4.

items.question: Why should we not boast about our own strength or willpower when we survive something?
items.text:
The books speak to this plainly. When people credited a man's survival to his resilience and willpower, he died suddenly a week later, and the question was asked, "Where was his strong will power?" [1]. God does not like it when you boast about things He has given you as though you did not receive them, as 1 Corinthians 4:7 says: "What hast thou that thou didst not receive? If thou didst receive it then why dost thou boast as though thou didst not receive it?" [1].

The books also warn that when a Christian keeps boasting about his strength, Satan hears him and decides to test him, and where you are over-confident is where you can be the weakest, because you have dropped your guard [2][3]. Staying on the right track is largely by the grace of God, not by your own strength, so "let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12) [2][3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 12 of *Those who are Proud*, chapter 3 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 5 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 1:20; 1 Corinthians 4:7; 1 Corinthians 10:12.

items.question: How should a pastor plan church finances when people don't pay the money they pledged?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak plainly to this. A wise pastor should not expect more than 30% of pledges to come in, and must never budget on what the congregation has pledged [1][2][6]. Pastors who budget on promised amounts are usually accused of misusing funds because the full amounts are never realized [1][2].

Instead, the build-up of your regular tithes and offerings should be the main source of project financing; fund-raising is only a boost to your existing financial situation, for God has determined that the church be financed through regular tithes and offerings [1][2][6]. It is also wise to save money towards a project before embarking on fund-raising, so that the project comes on whether the people pay up or not [1][2]. And if you do take pledges, the shorter the time given to honour them the higher the returns, so a period of one week to three months is recommended [2][6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 12 of *Church Growth* and chapter 6 of *Church Administration*.

items.question: How can we grow our church like the early church did?
items.text:
The early church grew as the apostles preached the word and the Lord added to the church daily, so that the number of disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem [1][3]. Growth like that is measurable — three thousand added in a day, then about five thousand men believing [3].

A bishop must carry out his duties with all his heart as unto the Lord, and church growth is a priority because Jesus said, "I will build my church and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" [1]. It is one of the most difficult things to do, and you must fight for it, making it one of the great ambitions of your life [2]. Set up a Church Growth Office to monitor the things that make churches grow — attendance, income, branches, lay and full-time pastors, shepherds, small groups, active members, weekly converts [3] — and grow your easily defined groups, the "tangerine segments" like the choir, ushers, or neighbourhood force, as engines of growth [6]. Do it through a systematic campaign of aggressive activities rather than expecting crowds to appear by osmosis [4]. And don't be in a hurry: the kingdom of God is like a mustard seed, the least of all seeds that becomes a great tree (Matthew 13:31, 32), and one pastor's church that began with a single member is now a megachurch [5][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 62 and 64 of *The Gift Of Governments*, chapter 11 of *Attempt Great Things for God*, chapters 4 and 26 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church*, chapter 7 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 20 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Jeremiah 30:19; Matthew 13:31-32; Acts 2:41; Acts 2:47; Acts 4:4; Acts 6:6-7; Acts 13:44; Acts 16:5.

items.question: Why do some pastors keep moving from place to place or stay far from home?
items.book: Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order
items.text:
Some pastors move because they are searching for the place God has designed for them, where they will become fruitful. Jacob recognized that the Lord was in a certain place, and Isaac moved from place to place until he found Rehoboth, saying, "now the Lord hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land" (Genesis 26:22) [1]. A bishop may also transfer pastors who cannot break through and flourish in a town, since a transfer may break a cycle of barrenness, and may move those unable to live in purity or holiness in that place [7].

But the books also describe other reasons. Some move from church to church to be where their history or background is not known, and separation from fellowship leaves a person without the voice of God or right advice [3]. Others move to escape trouble at home: one man of God lived a seven-hour flight away from his wife, and another abandoned his church and moved to another country, not for mission work but because, like Elijah, he was on the run [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 10 of *Opportunities*, chapter 59 of *The Gift Of Governments* and chapter 18 of *The Beauty The Beast and The Pastor*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 26:22; Genesis 28:16; 1 Kings 21:18-19; Matthew 16:26; Titus 1:5.

items.question: How old were Jesus' disciples when he called them?
items.text:
The books give us some clues here. From the Mishnah's stages of a young man's life, most of the disciples may have been below eighteen, with some as young as fifteen, since Peter is the only one known to have been married [1][3]. Peter himself likely started his ministry at about the age of twenty, since Jesus paid the temple tax for Peter and Himself but not the others, and only those twenty and up were counted for the tax (Exodus 30:12-14) [5]. The disciples were also apprentices in their family businesses, which suggests none was considered an outstanding Jewish scholar [4].

That said, the books also say there is no evidence in Scripture for a specific age for any of the disciples, and that these are clues and inferences rather than certainties [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *The Word Of My Patience*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 30:12-14; Matthew 8:14-15; Matthew 17:24-27; Luke 5:10; Acts 4:13; Revelation 3:10.

items.question: How can I deal with people in my church who criticize the pastor behind his back?
items.text:
Our books speak to this plainly. Criticism of the pastor behind his back is not a small thing — it is listed among the reasons people withhold their tithes, and such people hold an unspoken standard of living they expect their pastor never to cross [2]. One book goes so far as to say that a church filled with critical and faultfinding people is a church filled with demons, and that fighting against the pastor is one of the highest kinds of deception in the church [7].

The remedy given is not prayer or fasting but removal: "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out; yea strife and reproach shall cease" (Proverbs 22:10), and the book applies this directly — dismiss, expel, eject, banish, fire, sack, discard, unseat and lay off any scoffer in your set-up [4]. Yet another passage counsels patience, noting that criticism often comes from immaturity or inexperience, as when assistant pastors criticize a senior pastor because they have never been head pastors themselves; there the advice is to overlook it, check it before it grows into rebellion, and let the person go through the "school of hard knocks" by pioneering a church himself [5]. Jesus, after the disciples abandoned Him, did not rebuke them for betraying Him but sent them out to preach (Mark 14:27-31) [5].

So the books hold both a firm hand and a patient one, and I would not choose between them for you.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich*, chapters 4 and 7 of *Those Who Are Ignorant* and chapter 10 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 1:1; Proverbs 22:10; Proverbs 23:7; Proverbs 26:15; Mark 14:27-31; Romans 13:1.

items.question: What does the Bible say about people who were born and raised in the church?
items.text:
What a blessing it is to be born in the house of God. The eighty-seventh psalm speaks of the spiritual blessings that follow young people who were born in the house, and it says "this and that man was born in her: and the highest himself shall establish her" [2]. So those born in the house are going to be greatly established, and glorious things are spoken of them, as Psalm 87:3 says [1]. They will be counted among the great when the Lord writes up the people, as Psalm 87:6 says [1], and they will produce good music, for "as well the singers as the players on instruments shall be there," as Psalm 87:7 says [1].

Being born in a particular church and growing up in that church to become a leader in the same church is a prophetic blessing God is giving you [2]. If you were born in the church and grew up in the church, expect great things from God [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Ready@20*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 87:1-7.

items.question: How can I show appreciation to the people in my life before it's too late?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this plainly. Value people before you lose them, because when something is gone forever you suddenly realize how valuable it was [1][2]. The son who had said all he could say, and kissed his father goodbye on the day he travelled, had little to regret after he lost him [1][2]. So look into your life and see whether there is anybody you need to value, and if it is not too late, locate them and find a suitable way of expressing appreciation [1][2].

Honour before it is too late — rush to do it now, for greatness is often only recognized after a person dies [3]. And remember that God says if you keep wasting what He has given you, He will take it away; if He gives you a pastor and you don't value him, He will take him away, and if He gives you a mother and you are not grateful, He will take her away [1][2]. The deepest thanks is not words alone but a life given back: "The only way you can say, 'Thank you' is with your life" [5], a reasonable service offered to God [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 4 of *Frugality*, chapter 13 of *Those Who Honour You* and chapter 4 of *How Can I Say Thanks*.

Scriptures referenced: Romans 12:1-2.

items.question: How do I experience God's presence when I don't feel Him near?
items.text:
I hear the ache in that question, and I want to walk with you gently here. Our books say plainly that God is real and that it is possible to grow in your ability to experience Him — you can feel His presence in your room, in your meetings, at home [2][4]. So the dryness you feel is not the end of the story; the books treat knowing His presence as something you can grow in, like knowing Him as healer or provider [4].

They also point to some practical things. The presence of God is felt where salvation and redemption are preached — where the cross and the blood of Jesus are central — and it is not felt where those are set aside [1][5][8]. Being under a covering, humbly relating to the pastor or father God places over you, is also spoken of as a way the presence of God is experienced [3]. And sins of the flesh and sins of pride are named as reasons many have lost the sense of His presence [6].

One more thing the books say: His presence is like dew — invisible, yet you can see its effects in the watering and growth of your life [2]. So even when you cannot feel Him, look for the growth.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 13 and 18 of *The Anointing and the Presence* and chapters 11 and 14 of *Steps to God's Presence*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 33:14-15; Ezekiel 48:35; Hosea 14:5-6; Zechariah 11:12; Matthew 27:8-9; Luke 5:17; 1 Corinthians 1:27-29.

items.question: How can I keep from becoming bitter and turning away from God when I go through hard times?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this very thing, and the heart of it is this: suffering is a test, and it brings out what is in you [5]. When you receive what they call the contradiction of sinners — something contrary to what you expected after doing good — be careful, and do not turn against God [1]. Jesus Himself endured the contradiction of sinners and showed us how to endure it, as Hebrews 12:3 says [1].

Do not become bitter, and do not let bitterness move you away from God, for Hebrews 12:15 warns lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled [3]. When you walk in forgiveness you attract God's mercy, but when bitterness is in your spirit you will no longer receive from God and He no longer answers your prayers [2]. So maintain a sweet spirit and learn to live without bitterness [2]. Remember too that God led Israel to the bitter waters of Marah, and He knows why He brings you to a place of bitterness; do not fall away there, but survive it and go on, and you will become one of the few that are chosen [4]. And do not murmur or complain, for murmuring reveals a bad attitude and turns into bitterness [6]. Instead, put on the new man, in whom instead of bitterness there is forgiveness and love [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying*, chapter 10 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapters 26 and 30 of *Why Few Are Chosen* and chapter 2 of *Tasters And Partakers*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 8:2; Hebrews 12:3; Hebrews 12:15.

items.question: How can I pray more effectively?
items.text:
Prayer that works is not doodling and dawdling — it is effectual, fervent prayer, and James 5:16 says the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much [1]. So let your prayers be guided by the Word of God, praying the very prayers recorded in Scripture, like the prayers in Ephesians 1:17-19 and Ephesians 3:15-19 [1]. Pray fervently — ardently, with passion and feeling, so that anyone watching could describe your prayer as burning and eager [3]. Spend hours praying in tongues, as Paul boasted, "I thank God that I speak in tongues more than you all" (1 Corinthians 14:18) [3]. And make prayer a two-way affair, speaking to the Holy Spirit and hearing His voice, for as Jesus said, the Comforter "shall teach you all things" (John 14:26) [3].

Prayer is also meant to be habitual and constant — 1 Thessalonians 5:17 tells us to pray without ceasing, on the bus, in the office, in the shower [4]. It is important to enter your closet and pray alone, for there is a difference between praying alone and praying with a group [6]. And develop the ability to pray four times a day: morning, afternoon, evening, and all-the-time [6]. Jesus Himself rose a great while before day and went to a solitary place to pray (Mark 1:35) [6][8], and He continued all night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12,13) [6]. Watching and praying — staying awake at night to pray — is more important than fasting and praying, and those who learn it become mighty prayer warriors [8].

items.question: If I do good things for others, how will I be rewarded?
items.book: He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this in two ways, and I'll give you both.

First, your reward is not to be looked for from the people you help. A leader looks to God for rewards, for "whatsoever good thing any man doeth, the same shall he receive of the Lord, whether he be bond or free" (Ephesians 6:8) [2]. So do not expect much from people; expect your rewards from God [2][7]. People are often ungrateful and forgetful, and even those you have blessed may repay you with evil, as Jeremiah found when they dug a pit for him (Jeremiah 18:20) [1][4][7]. Do not be surprised by this, and do not retaliate, for if you begin to retaliate because of ingratitude, you will lose your place in the ministry [2].

Second, there is a reward in the work itself. God has seen your faithfulness with what belongs to others, and He rewards that faithfulness with more work — being given your own, as Luke 16:12 says, "if ye have not been faithful in that which is another man's, who shall give you that which is your own?" [5]. And be careful to obey rather than merely do good deeds that impress others, for God will not reward you because you did many good things but because you obeyed Him [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How Can I Say Thanks*, chapter 101 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 26 of *The Art of Hearing*, chapter 5 of *WOM15. The Reward for Hard Work is More Work* and chapter 5 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 26:27; Jeremiah 18:19-20; Luke 14:26; Luke 16:12; John 10:32; Ephesians 6:8; 2 Timothy 3:1-2.

items.question: Why do the people closest to a pastor, like family and his wife, often have a hard time receiving from his ministry?
items.text:
This is a painful thing, and our books speak to it plainly: it is the problem of familiarity. Jesus Himself could do no mighty work in His hometown, and they were offended at Him, saying, "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" (Mark 6:1-3, 5) [6]. Moses, who commanded a pillar of fire and a pillar of cloud, could not impress his own sister Miriam [6].

Relatives suffer from familiarity too, saying, "Is this not Azoyzoy's son? We carried him when he was a baby" [8]. And pastors' wives often suffer from severe familiarity; like Michal, they are not impressed with their husbands when everyone else is impressed, saying, "I know you. No one knows you better than I do" [8]. The book notes they are right about these things, but the fact is they have become victims of familiarity [8]. Familiarity even carves out a road of ministry for anointed people, directing them away from colleagues, friends and family toward the non-familiar, the poor, the forgotten and the neglected [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *Church Planting* and chapter 13 of *Ministerial Barrenness*.

Scriptures referenced: Mark 6:1-3; Mark 6:5.

items.question: I keep saying hurtful things when I am angry. How do I control my mouth?
items.text:
The books speak to this. Agape love is not rude or easily provoked, and angry outbursts are not likely to change the other person — they may only cause them to withdraw [1]. Scripture says, "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying" (Ephesians 4:29), and "Neither give place to the devil" (Ephesians 4:27) [1][6].

On control itself, the Bible says no man can tame his tongue; it takes the Holy Spirit to help the believer control it [3]. The tongue is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison (James 3:8), and death and life are in the power of the tongue (Proverbs 18:21) [3][7]. So deal with it quickly, as you would poison [3]. Also, anger and wrath are signs of lingering unforgiveness, and we are told to put away bitterness, wrath, anger, clamour and evil speaking, being kind and tenderhearted, forgiving one another (Ephesians 4:31-32) [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 60 of *Model Marriage*, chapter 1 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue*, chapter 4 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition* and chapter 2 of *Seven Great Principles*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 18:21; 2 Corinthians 10:5; Galatians 5:13; Ephesians 4:26-27; Ephesians 4:29; Ephesians 4:31-32; James 3:8.

items.question: How can I stay close to God and keep bearing fruit in my life?
items.text:
Draw near to God and He will draw near to you (James 4:8) — that is the heart of it. Abiding in Christ means staying in God, not being in and out; as John 15:5 says, he that abides in Him brings forth much fruit, and the longer you stay in God, the more fruitful you become [1]. Closeness is a law of fruit bearing: as the branch cannot bear fruit of itself except it abide in the vine, so it is with you (John 15:4-5) [3].

Staying connected to Jesus is the master key; without Him you can do nothing (John 15:5), and except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it (Psalm 127:1) [2]. So watch your connection to the tree, for disconnection and detachment are the master keys to withering, while close attachment leads to life [4][5]. Keep pressing through the valleys too, for just after the valley is a prepared table, and except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abides alone; but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit (John 12:24) [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Fruitfulness (2022)*, chapter 6 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make*, chapter 14 of *Victory Secrets* and chapter 8 of *TS2. Hope Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 23:5-6; Psalms 127:1; Mark 12:34; John 12:24; John 15:4-6; James 4:8; Revelation 1:20.

items.question: How can I be sure I really know the Lord and won't be turned away from heaven?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this very thing, and the heart of it is whether you truly know the Lord and are known by Him. Jesus uses His personal knowledge of you as a basis for judgment, and not knowing God is the basis for being thrown out of heaven [1]. Many serve the Lord without knowing Him in reality, and one day people will say, "Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name?" only to hear, "I never knew you: depart from me" (Matthew 7:22-23) [2][3].

The way the books point to is a personal relationship with Him, and they say a daily quiet time is what makes that possible — nothing else can give you a personal relationship with the Lord, and a daily quiet time will prevent you from going to hell [3][4]. It is up to you to draw near to Him daily, for as James 4:8 says, "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you" [4]. Through the blood of Jesus you are cleansed from your sins and can get to know God [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Weeping and Gnashing*, chapter 30 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*, chapter 4 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day* and chapter 5 of *The Secret*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 7:21-23; Luke 13:25-28; 2 Timothy 1:8-9; James 4:8; Revelation 3:20.

items.question: What does the wind of the Holy Spirit do in a person's life?
items.text:
Friend, the books describe many things the wind of the Spirit does in a life. It blows away death, as when God made a wind to pass over the earth and the waters assuaged (Genesis 8:1-3) [1]. It makes a way for you when you seem trapped, as the Lord caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind (Exodus 14:21) [1][3]. It causes anything that displeases God to wither, like the seven ears blasted with the east wind (Genesis 41:22-23) [2], and it drives away demonic powers, as the Lord turned a mighty strong west wind which took away the locusts (Exodus 10:16-19) [2].

It also dries up the evil springs of the enemy, as Hosea 13:15 says the wind of the Lord shall come up and his spring shall become dry [3], and it can destroy the enemy's forces, for the Lord said He would raise up a destroying wind against Babylon (Jeremiah 51:1-2) [5]. It brings in the supplies you need, as through the wind of the Spirit Moses fed two million people [5]. And when the breath of God comes into you, you receive life: you begin to see, hear, and feel [6][7], there is activity [7], and there is growth [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 6 of *Flow in the Anointing*.

items.question: What can I learn from Esther about helping others even when I'm comfortable?
items.text:
Friend, the books have a great deal to say about this. Esther was favoured, chosen, and married by the king, living with every privilege imaginable, yet she was reminded that there were "others" outside the palace in great danger [2]. Her uncle Mordecai warned her that if she held her peace, deliverance would arise from another place, but she and her father's house would be destroyed — and who knew whether she had come to the kingdom for such a time as this [5][8].

The books press the point that your comfort and position have a reason: perhaps God made you the queen so you could help "others," and you were raised up to deliver them [1]. Esther hesitated at first, explaining the rules of the palace and the risk, but the books note that many successful people come up with excuses about why they cannot help [5]. In the end she called for fasting and said, "if I perish, I perish" [7], and she is remembered not because she was a queen — there have been many queens — but because she helped "others" [1].

The books also warn plainly: destruction is waiting for those who forget about "others," and your family too may be affected if you neglect them [8]. And a daughter of destiny will not quickly forget where she came from; she remembers her father and helps him [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Others*, chapter 33 of *Daughter, You Can Make It* and chapter 14 of *The Art of Following*.

Scriptures referenced: Esther 4:13-16.

items.question: Why is it so hard to leave a church that feels like family?
items.text:
It's hard because a church that feels like family really has become family. Jesus stretched out His hand toward His disciples and said, "Whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother" (Matthew 12:48-50), and so those who obey God's word are made His family [1]. When leadership builds the church as a family, no one leaves a family — it is difficult to leave your family, and difficult to leave a church that has become a family [1].

Every family has its problems; there are conflicts and misunderstandings, but there is simply no way you can leave your family — you are part of it whether you like it or not, and a misunderstanding with your uncle does not lead you to change your name [2]. So members are taught that misunderstandings and hurts should not make them change their churches, but that family members belong together in a lifetime commitment [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Be Thou Faithful Unto Death* and chapter 11 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 5:5; Matthew 12:48-50; 1 Corinthians 3:9; Ephesians 5:31.

items.question: Can God heal emotional wounds and mental problems that medicine can't fix?
items.book: Amplify Your Ministry with Miracles And Manifestations Of The Holy Spirit
items.text:
Yes, friend, the books speak to this clearly and with great hope. A daily dose of God's powerful Word brings healing to every inner wound, and God's Word is described as medicine to all your flesh, as Psalm 107:20 and Proverbs 4:20-22 are cited [1]. The Lord Himself says, "I am the Lord your doctor, the Lord your healer, the Lord your physician" — Jehovah Rophe [2]. He heals the broken in heart and binds up their wounds, as Psalm 147:3 says [3][6], and Jesus came specifically to heal the brokenhearted, as Luke 4:18 declares [4]. The books note that medicines often only sedate or improve mood, and that God can heal what man cannot heal [2][3].

That said, the books also warn against extremes: God is not against medicine, and the wisdom for medical science is from Him — Christ is both the power and the wisdom of God, as 1 Corinthians 1:24 says [5][8]. So the two streams of healing are ordained of God and are not contrary to each other [5]. One book adds that while God's grace is available for your emotional healing, you are the key to your own recovery, and it walks through stages from shock to healing, including forgiveness [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapters 1, 15 and 17 of *Amplify Your Ministry with Miracles And Manifestations Of The Holy Spirit* and chapter 59 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Kings 2:19-22; Psalms 23:3; Psalms 107:20; Psalms 147:3; Jeremiah 17:14; Mark 5:2-3; Luke 4:18; John 9:1-2; 1 Corinthians 1:24.

items.question: How can I spend time with God every morning without getting bored?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
What a good question, and our books speak to it warmly. The heart of it is that a quiet time is not a duty to endure but a relationship to enjoy: during quiet time you develop the most important relationship of your life, and a natural relationship develops between any two people who spend quality time together [2]. You draw near to God and He draws near to you, as James 4:8 says [2].

Practically, the books point to feeding your spirit on the Word rather than trying to manufacture a feeling. Allow the Word to enter your spirit through a daily Quiet Time, Bible study and Bible reading, and let it be like the sincere milk of the Word that makes you grow, as 1 Peter 2:2 says [1]. A daily dose of the Word will increase your faith [7], and a daily quiet time drives away weariness, dejection and depression — the Word is like rain and snow that cools and refreshes, as Isaiah 55:10 says [7]. Jesus Himself prayed at dawn, rising a great while before day and going to a solitary place, as Mark 1:35 shows [4], and praying at dawn will help you read your Bible and grow in the Word [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How to be Born again & Avoid Hell*, chapters 3 and 6 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day* and chapter 13 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 3:1-3; Isaiah 55:10; Mark 1:34-36; Romans 1:16; Romans 10:17; James 4:8; 1 Peter 2:2.

items.question: How can I tell if someone is really a Christian or just going to church?
items.text:
That's a question the books speak to plainly. We can distinguish genuine Christians from counterfeit Christians by looking at their fruits, as Matthew 7:20 says, "Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them" [1][2][3][4]. If, by your spiritual activity, others just like you are brought to the Lord and discipled, then this fruit shows that you are real; but if you have no converts to show for your Christianity, then there must be something missing [1][2][3].

The books also warn that church membership does not prove you are a genuine Christian at all, and that many who go to church are not born again and do not even know God [1][2][4][5]. Real Christianity takes place outside the church after Sundays, with each weekday having its share of prayer, worship, Bible reading and labouring for the Lord [1][5]. So the counsel given is to examine yourself, whether you be in the faith, as 2 Corinthians 13:5 says [1][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *Many Are Called* and chapter 3 of *Bearing Fruit After Your Kind*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 7:20; 2 Corinthians 13:5.

items.question: Why can't I get to heaven by being a good person?
items.text:
Being a good person and doing good works is not the way to Heaven; good works will not take you there [1][2][7]. As Isaiah 64:6 says, all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags, and there is none righteous, no, not one [1][2][3]. We are saved by grace through faith, not of works, lest any man should boast (Ephesians 2:8-9) [3][7]. The only way is through the blood of Jesus [1][2][7].

That said, the same passage that says we are not saved by works also says we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God has before ordained that we should walk in them (Ephesians 2:8-10) [3][4]. So good works do not save us, but after we are saved, God has good works for us to do [3][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 65 and 111 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*, chapter 1 of *Tell Them* and chapters 2 and 3 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 11:16; Proverbs 11:4-5; Isaiah 42:17; Isaiah 64:6; Matthew 7:21-22; Matthew 15:8; Mark 7:6-7; Luke 9:24; Acts 4:12; Romans 3:10 and 3 more.

items.question: What happens if I dishonour my husband?
items.text:
The books speak plainly to this, and it is a sobering word. Dishonour causes you to lose your place and be replaced, as Vashti lost her position and was replaced by a more humble person — the reward for dishonour is to lose your place [1][3]. Dishonour also brings a demonic invasion: when Vashti dishonoured her husband, the devils of demotion invaded her life, and Judas received the devil into his soul when he dishonoured the appointment Jesus gave him [2]. And dishonour brings obscurity — "Whoso curseth his father or his mother, his lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness" (Proverbs 20:20), so that you become unimportant and insignificant [6].

There is also this mystery of the marriage covenant: when your husband is disgraced, you are disgraced as well; when his face is dragged in the mud, so is yours [5]. So wives must not blacken the reputation of their husbands, though it is all right to seek help from counsellors or pastors — a fine balance must be achieved between openness for obtaining advice and humiliating your husband [5]. And when the awe and honour a wife had at the beginning are gone, she stops washing, cleaning, anointing herself and concerning herself with what she wears at home; the woman who does not adapt herself to her husband is dishonouring him [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 6 and 11 of *Those Who Honour You* and chapter 31 of *Daughter, You Can Make It*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 32:17; Ruth 3:1-4; 1 Samuel 2:30; Esther 1:15-20; Proverbs 20:20; Luke 22:3; John 8:49-50.

items.question: Why does the Bible warn against trying to get rich?
items.book: Labour to be blessed…labour not to be rich
items.text:
The books give several reasons. Ill-gotten riches can cut your life short — "he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days" (Jeremiah 17:10-11) [1]. Earthly riches can turn you into a fool, as in the parable of the man with full barns to whom God said, "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee" (Luke 12:16-21) [1][2]. Riches can prevent you from taking up your cross and following Jesus; Jesus said, "How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!" (Mark 10:17-23) [5]. Riches are deceptive and can deceive you — "the deceitfulness of riches... choke the word" (Mark 4:19) [5]. And they are linked to many temptations and traps: "they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evil" (1 Timothy 6:9-10) [3][4].

The counsel is not to aim at riches but at the blessing, since "the blessing of the Lord makes rich" (Proverbs 10:22) [6], and within that blessing you will have more than enough and to spare [2][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 4 of *Labour to be blessed…labour not to be rich* and chapter 2 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 10:22; Proverbs 23:4; Ecclesiastes 5:14-16; Jeremiah 17:10-11; Matthew 1:21; Mark 4:19; Mark 10:17-23; Luke 12:15-21; 1 Timothy 6:9-10.

items.question: How do I meditate on the Bible and get something out of it during my quiet time?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
What a good thing to want, pastor. The books say plainly that if you do not think about what you are reading, you will lose a major blessing of the Word of God, and Paul told Timothy to think about the Word of God — "Consider what I say; and the Lord give thee understanding in all things" (2 Timothy 2:7) [1][2][3].

Practically, they counsel you to read the passage slowly, not to read a very long passage unless it is necessary, and to stop at any verse that strikes you and think about it — God's Word is so powerful that a single word in a verse is enough to change your life, so each quiet time should be a search for that single word [1][2][3]. Think about the meanings of the words you are reading, and think about how the Scripture applies to life in your generation [1][2][3]. Whisper to the Holy Spirit, saying, "Help me Holy Spirit to understand your Word. Father, give me the Spirit of Wisdom and Revelation," as Ephesians 1:17 prays [1][2][3]. Then decide on a practical way to implement what you have learned, for without thinking of a way to apply the Scripture directly you will often not benefit from your quiet time [1][2][6]. One of the books adds that you should stay there and turn it over in your mind till the full revelation comes to you [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapter 8 of *Key Facts for New Believers*, chapter 3 of *The Secret* and chapter 10 of *One Thousand Micro Churches*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 119:18; Ephesians 1:17; 2 Timothy 2:7.

items.question: How can I cooperate with the anointing for dreams and visions?
items.text:
The key is to accept, believe in, and flow with the visions and dreams God gives you, rather than despising them [1]. Daniel wrote his dream down because he respected it, and writing something down shows how seriously you take it [1]. So don't dismiss a dream just because it seems vague or strange — we all have vague and unclear dreams from the Lord, and the drive to obey them is the drive toward the anointing [2].

Obey what you're given: if we obeyed the visions and dreams God gave us, we would experience the anointing, and each one takes you a step closer [2]. Flow with your dreams and visions, because they are God's instruments encouraging you along the road to the anointing [3]. Be careful, though, not to be moved by dreams you generate out of your own needs and desires — hungry people dream about food and thirsty people dream about drink — so wait on the Lord for genuine dreams and visions [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 15 of *The Art of Following*, chapter 6 of *Steps to the Anointing* and chapter 18 of *How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Job 4:13; Daniel 7:1-4; Acts 10:7-8; Acts 10:13-15; Acts 10:32; Acts 10:48.

items.question: How do I get angels to intervene in my situation when I pray?
items.text:
Friend, our books speak to this plainly: prayer itself is the way angels are released into your situation. Jesus said He could pray to the Father and be given more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:52-54), and the book says prayer is the greatest and most definite way of securing angelic participation [1]. Where there is prayer there is angelic activity — prayer activates and releases angels [2].

The examples bear this out. An angel came to Zachariah with the words "thy prayer is heard" (Luke 1:13) [2][8]; angels ministered to Jesus in the wilderness as He prayed (Mark 1:13) [3]; an angel strengthened Him in Gethsemane as He prayed (Luke 22:43) [3][6]; Peter was delivered from prison while many were gathered together praying (Acts 12) [4]; and Cornelius was told his prayers had come up as a memorial before God (Acts 10) [4]. So expect angelic intervention because of your many prayers — your heart's desire will be answered by the intervention of angels [2][8].

One other way the book names is hospitality: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares," as with Lot and Abraham, for angels go where they are fed [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 6 of *Prayer Changes Things*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 19:1-3; Daniel 10:1-15; Matthew 26:52-54; Luke 1:8-16; Luke 22:40-44; Acts 12:1-12; Revelation 15:1.

items.question: How should I respond when people constantly accuse and criticize me for serving God?
items.book: One of You is a Devil
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this directly, and the first thing they say is that you are not alone in it. Everyone who takes up the call of God is truly an honourable person, and yet ministers are vilified and denigrated constantly; Moses and our Lord Jesus both sustained relentless attacks in the form of complaints and accusations [6]. Jesus was perfect, and yet He was accused until His life was snuffed out [6].

So how do you respond? David gives us a picture. When Michal accused him over his worship, he disagreed with her decisively and refused to accept that kind of talk in his house, saying it was before the LORD who chose him, and he would play before the LORD [8]. The book adds that this would be the end of many wives of ministers if ministers would respond that decisively to accusations [8]. At the same time, be careful not to let the accusations push you into something you would not otherwise do — Moses finally erred in ministry when he responded to the complaints of the people, for accusations push people to do things they would not have done [6]. And do not let fear of the accuser keep you from obeying the call, for fear is an evil spirit, and those who follow it will weep and gnash their teeth in heaven for being afraid of serving God [3].

There is also a word about weighing accusations rather than swallowing every one: against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses (1 Timothy 5:19), and loyalty demands continuous analysis in the face of constant accusations, rumours and slanderous stories [7]. The book also warns against being the one who points the finger, since accusations are called "the pointing of the finger," and your light will break forth like the dawn and there will be recovery if you put away the pointing of the finger (Isaiah 58:8-9) [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 5 and 8 of *Those Who Accuse You*, chapter 5 of *Weeping and Gnashing* and chapter 4 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 6:20; Isaiah 58:8-9; Daniel 10:13; Matthew 25:24; 1 Timothy 5:19.

items.question: Can a pastor lead a group of people he pulled away from their church into a new one?
items.text:
Our books speak directly to this. The question every rebel leader must be asked is, "Can you lead these people?" and the answer given is no — the people you lead will never be loyal to you, because they have learned how to rebel and overthrow legitimate authority, and they will practise it again when they get the chance [1]. You will not be able to silence their rebellious way of speaking, quench their murmurings, or prevent the hatred and conspiracies around you, because you have sown the seeds of instability and rebellion and taught your followers how to dislodge legitimate leaders [1].

The books also show this working out in practice: a pastor who broke away and started his own church near the one he had led saw others follow his example, and a "domino spirit of rebellion" was released into the team of pastors [2]. In another case, a pastor who left the majority of the old congregation with his associate later had that associate steal the hearts of the people and lead them to break away from him [4]. And where a breakaway leader appointed eleven new pastors, the book calls this the typical move of renegade ministers, ordaining men of the lowest sort as Jeroboam did, which makes nonsense of spiritual authority and confuses the flock [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 5, 6 and 10 of *Those who leave you*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 12:28-31.

items.question: Why are Jesus' words so much greater than the words of other great teachers?
items.book: The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make
items.text:
The books say the words of Jesus are the words of the Son of God, and no other man ever spoke like He did; His words have outlasted any other words spoken by any other person [3][4]. Where other teachers give truths mingled with what is trivial and absurd, He eliminated the trivial, the temporal, and the false, selecting just the eternal and the universal [8]. His words are anointed, so that they changed the lives of those who heard them, and they are full of love and kindness [5]. They answer the great questions that throb in the human breast — who is God, does He love me, how can I be forgiven, where will I go when I die — as no other man's words can [1][7].

The difference is not merely one of degree: after reading Plato, Socrates or Aristotle, we feel the difference between their words and Christ's is the difference between an enquiry and a revelation [5]. His words have passed into law, doctrines, proverbs and consolations, but they have never passed away, and no human teacher ever dared to claim eternity for his words [1][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *The Words of Jesus* and chapter 5 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 12:36; Matthew 18:21-22; Luke 4:36; John 6:63; John 7:46.

items.question: How do I know if God has hidden a gift in me that others can't see yet?
items.book: Lord I Know You Need Somebody
items.text:
What you're describing is exactly what these books speak to. Every great man of God is like a hidden treasure yet to be revealed, and God is the One who has concealed the potential He placed in you [1]. Your ministry is like a hidden seed planted in a field that will grow into a mighty tree, or like a little leaven hidden in a meal that will eventually influence the whole dough [1].

So the fact that people cannot see it yet is not a sign it isn't there. Even Mary could not see the gift of God in Jesus, and His own brothers did not believe in Him (John 7:1-5) [2]. Joseph's father rebuked him and could not see the treasure in him (Genesis 37:9-10) [3][4]. Do not be sad or angry when those closest to you don't notice or appreciate who you are; with time, the hidden gift God placed in you will become apparent [2][3].

One caution from the books: while God hides the gift, there are also hidden things in us that must be corrected, like jealousy, hatred, unforgiveness, or bitterness, which no one can see but will destroy your life and ministry [5]. So ask yourself what hidden aspect of your life is missing or faulty, and give yourself to the hidden things like prayer and fasting, which your Father who sees in secret will reward openly (Matthew 6:6) [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Lord I Know You Need Somebody* and chapter 12 of *Why Few Are Chosen*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 37:9-10; Matthew 6:6; Matthew 13:31-32; Matthew 13:44-46; John 7:1-5.

items.question: Why does God allow trials and suffering in the lives of believers?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this directly, and they give several reasons God allows His people to suffer.

Suffering is appointed to believers, not accidental: "For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake" (Philippians 1:29), and we are told we are appointed thereunto (1 Thessalonians 3:3) [5]. It pleases God to allow it, as Isaiah 53:10 says, "it pleased the Lord to bruise him" [4]. It proves you are a good Christian, since Paul laboured and suffered reproach because he trusted in the living God (1 Timothy 4:10), and "all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution" (2 Timothy 3:12) [2]. It follows the example of Jesus, who suffered for us "leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps" (1 Peter 2:21) [3]. It breaks the power of sin, for "he that hath suffered in the flesh hath ceased from sin" (1 Peter 4:1) [3]. It tests and humbles you, as Deuteronomy 8:2 says God led Israel in the wilderness to humble them and test what was in their heart [8]. And it goes along with your specific calling, as Paul said he suffered these things because he was appointed a preacher and apostle (2 Timothy 1:11), and the Lord said of Paul, "I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name's sake" (Acts 9:15-16) [1].

One caution the books add: a minister should suffer only according to the will of God, for there are two possible reasons for what you experience — you may be suffering according to His will, or suffering the fruits of your own disobedience, so it is important to seek God about why you are going through what you are going through [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying* and chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 47:9; Deuteronomy 8:2; Isaiah 53:10; Acts 9:15-16; 2 Corinthians 1:9; 2 Corinthians 12:7; Ephesians 5:2; Philippians 1:29; 1 Thessalonians 3:3; 1 Timothy 4:10 and 6 more.
