items.question: And how should I deal with them once I notice it?
items.text:
Friend, the books say disloyalty doesn't happen overnight — becoming disloyal is a process, and most people are unaware of it, so learn to detect it both to kill any such tendency in yourself and to see it in those you work with [1]. The first stage is an independent spirit: the person is still part of the church but does what he wants in spite of contrary instructions, obeying only the instructions he thinks are important [1]. Later stages include inflexibility — the stubborn, defiant person who won't go beyond what is stipulated, won't adapt, and won't take correction when confronted, like Saul arguing with Samuel [3]. Watch too for the one who mocks or scorns your cause [2], and for questionable loyalty, which is diagnosed when a person makes malicious, damaging or poisonous comments, or has a spouse, close relative, friendship or communication with someone openly disloyal [7].

As for dealing with them, the books give several methods. The first is the teaching method — teaching the Word of God regularly as a preventive process, because teaching fights against deception, and it is only deceived people who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer [6]. The biblical treatment for a mocker is expulsion: whenever you realize someone is mocking you, do not hesitate to expel him from your life [2]. People who cause divisions must be marked and avoided, as Romans 16:17-18 says [2]. The scorner is to be cast out, as Proverbs 22:10 says, "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out; yea, strife and reproach shall cease" [7][8]. Even longstanding workers who are disloyal, disobedient or non-compliant should be dismissed completely, though in keeping with mercy and compassion financial provisions should be made so they can live and work elsewhere without undue hardship, and so the root of bitterness does not spread, as Hebrews 12:15 warns [5]. Failure to dismiss someone who must go is weak leadership — like allowing a snake to live under your children's bed [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1 and 2 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*, chapters 7 and 12 of *Those Who Are Ignorant* and chapter 77 of *The Gift Of Governments*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 22:10; Romans 16:17-18; Hebrews 12:15.

items.question: How can I know what my calling from God is?
items.book: What It Means to Become a Shepherd
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and gently. One way is to watch what works: you see and know things about your calling, and you discover it by observing what the Lord does with you and your life, flowing with what God is doing rather than waiting for a voice thundering from Heaven [1]. Your calling is also according to God's purpose, so it is worth seeking to know the purpose within the call, not just the title [2].

You should also be filled with the knowledge of His will concerning your calling, since you can only be a teacher or sing because it is God's will for your life [3]. And a divine call is often accompanied by a supernatural desire and interest in the work of the ministry, which is a symptom of that call within [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Rules of Church Work (2nd Edition)*, chapter 1 of *Predestination*, chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing* and chapter 3 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 10:6; Romans 10:1; 1 Corinthians 1:1; 1 Corinthians 1:26; 2 Corinthians 1:1; Colossians 1:9; 2 Timothy 1:9; Hebrews 5:4.

items.question: How can I be a good shepherd to the people in my church?
items.text:
What a good thing to want, pastor. The books say plainly: if you are going to be a pastor, be a good one, doing it with all your might, as Ecclesiastes 9:10 says [2]. And they point to Jesus' own words in John 10 as the picture of what a good shepherd does.

Lead the way yourself. Anything you want your sheep to do, you must do it first, so they see you and follow, just as John 10:4 says the shepherd goes before them and the sheep follow because they know his voice [1][2]. Be practically available for them to see and learn from you in every area of life and ministry [2]. Let them know you too — open up your life so they are not following a mystery figure, and let them see you face the same problems and temptations they do [3]. Know your sheep, and don't let any slip away; Jesus said of those the Father gave Him, "none of them is lost" (John 17:12) [3].

Be deeply involved in evangelism, for that is the only way to be a good shepherd — leave the ninety-nine and go after the lost one, as Luke 15:4-7 describes [4][5]. Provide salvation for your sheep and give them life through your teaching, for Jesus said He came that they might have life more abundantly (John 10:10) [5]. Notice when your sheep are in trouble, and pray for their deliverance from witchcraft, demons and diseases, anointing them with oil [6]. And give your life for the sheep, as John 10:11 says the good shepherd does — the rank of a shepherd is carved out by the sacrifices he makes for his congregation [5][6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 27 of *The Art of Shepherding*, chapter 13 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapter 8 of *Church Growth* and chapter 2 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

items.question: How can I serve closely in ministry without missing the spiritual blessings?
items.text:
Draw near and stay near, because being close is both an art and an act of humility, and God promises that when you draw near to Him, He will draw near to you (James 4:8) [8]. When you are involved in personal service, make sure you get the "good part" — the good part of personal ministry is not the physical advantage but the spiritual treasure, as Mary chose that good part which would not be taken from her (Luke 10:41-42) [1][2]. Be careful of being unspiritual around a spiritual person, for many who work closely with a man of God miss the spiritual treasures of close fellowship [1][2].

Soak in the words of your spiritual father, as Elisha soaked in the words of Elijah and stayed close to the very end until the anointing he desired was flowing through his ministry (2 Kings 2:11) [5]. And understand the dangers of familiarity, for through familiarity Jesus' own family did not believe in Him (John 7:5) [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Rules of Church Work (2nd Edition)*, chapter 5 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 16 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Kings 2:11; Ezekiel 2:2; Mark 3:14; Luke 10:41-42; John 6:63; John 7:5; John 13:20; James 4:8.

items.question: How can I protect my church from wolves?
items.text:
The books give several ways. Be a pastor on fire: fire, passion and zeal are killers of wolves, and the power of deception and wickedness cannot stand against the power of the Holy Ghost and fire [1]. Fight aggressively, showing wolves that you are too dangerous to attack, and teach against every type of disloyalty until every wolf is exposed [5]. Expect wolves and prepare for them, teaching loyalty and faithfulness, since churches that do not will struggle to survive a wolf attack [4]. You can also place spiritual barriers: Paul spoke a curse against anyone bringing a false gospel, and the Lord told one pastor to place a curse for the protection of the church when he could not physically protect the sheep [2]. And identify sympathisers of the "departee" and send them away, as Abraham sent Ishmael away from Isaac (Genesis 25:5-6) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 4 of *Those Who are Wolves* and chapter 10 of *Those who leave you*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 25:5-6; Psalms 31:18; Luke 3:16; 1 Timothy 6:12; 1 Peter 5:8.

items.question: Why do I need to hear from God for myself instead of just listening to my pastor?
items.text:
You need to hear from God for yourself because hearing Him directly is how you come to know Him — the more you hear from God, the more you know Him, and people are rejected because Jesus never knew them (Matthew 7:22-23) [1]. You may be in a good church with a good pastor leading the flock, but you will still need to hear the voice of God for yourself; if you do not hear from God directly you will get disconnected [1]. The children of Israel were brought to Mount Sinai to hear God's voice for themselves, and they failed that test [1]. You need to know God for yourself and not just through a second person [1].

At the same time, the books also teach that you should listen to the messages of your leader — to learn how to preach, as Hebrews 6:12 says to be followers of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises, and to use their messages as resource material to give you things to preach [2]. Listening to preaching is itself a way God's word comes to you, and faith giants are created by hearing [8]. So both are held up: hearing God for yourself [1], and learning from the messages of your leader [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Not A Novice*, chapter 4 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 33 of *Faith Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 20:19-21; Psalms 23:1; Matthew 7:22-23; Hebrews 6:12.

items.question: How do I deal with betrayal in the church?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this — betrayal in ministry is a real wound, and the books speak to it plainly.

First, know that it should not surprise you. Betrayal is part of ministry and part of life; if you have not yet experienced it, you will, and it comes from people supposedly close to you [3]. Jesus Himself was betrayed, and Paul too — how can it be that you will not experience the same? [4] As Psalm 41:9 says, "mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me" [3]. If Judas is anything to go by, one out of twelve may be disloyal [4].

As for dealing with it, the books say you must be fierce and resolute, not dealing with the enemy in a spirit of benevolence, because disloyalty can end a church and a ministry [7]. Jesus called the disloyal Judas a devil, and pastors who take disloyalty lightly live to regret it [1][2]. The pattern given is what God did to the devil — bound him, shut him up, and set a seal on him (Revelation 20:1-3) [6]. Yet another method urged is preventive teaching of the Word, which fights deception, since it is the deceived who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *JUDAS
Who is he??*, chapter 2 of *One of You is a Devil*, chapter 5 of *Church Growth*, chapter 54 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 12 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapter 33 of *Victory Secrets* and chapter 12 of *The Church Must Send or It Will End*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 18:7-9; 2 Chronicles 32:25; Psalms 41:9; John 6:70-71; Revelation 20:1-3.

items.question: What does the Bible say about enjoying the money and blessings God gives you?
items.book: Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich
items.text:
Yes, the books speak to this. Ecclesiastes 6:1-2 is cited to show it is an evil thing to have riches, wealth and honour from God yet lack the power to eat thereof, so spend money on yourself and use some of the wealth you have earned on yourself as part of enjoying your working life [4]. Failure to eat your portion will make you hate life and hate work [4].

The books also say God takes pleasure in the prosperity of His servant, and that when you serve Him you will spend your days in prosperity, as Job 36:11-12 says [6]. And the blessing of the Lord makes rich and adds no sorrow, as Proverbs 10:22 says [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 9 of *Rules of Church Work (2nd Edition)* and chapter 6 of *It Is A Great Thing To Serve The Lord*.

items.question: How important is it to actually obey what Jesus says?
items.text:
It matters more than we can say, pastor. All through the Bible, believing is equated with obeying — to believe in the gospel is to pledge yourself to obey the commandments of God, and obeying the gospel is all that God expects from us [4]. Jesus Himself promised that He would manifest Himself to those who obey Him, and that He and the Father would come and make their abode with them, as John 14:21-25 says [2].

Obedience is also the sign of your love, and it provokes the anointing; there will be no manifestation towards those who do not obey [2]. And a novice must learn the importance of obeying commandments, because inexperienced people do not know how important it is to obey — that is why it is important to just obey every single commandment [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Not A Novice*, chapter 8 of *The Anointed and His Anointing* and chapter 2 of *Faith Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 10:12-13; Matthew 22:36-40; John 14:21-25; 2 Thessalonians 1:7-9; 1 Peter 4:17.

items.question: How can I recognize when someone has gone from just being disloyal into open rebellion against God's servants?
items.text:
The books describe this as a process, not a sudden event. Disloyalty begins subtly with an independent spirit, where a person is still part of the church but does what he wants in spite of contrary instructions [4]. It then moves through stages until it reaches open rebellion, which is the last stage of disloyalty — where a person openly attacks an authority figure he should rather honour [3].

At that open stage, the behaviour becomes bizarre and inappropriate: they may openly attack someone they previously hailed and honoured, insult and accuse someone they loved before, dishonour dignitaries, and spread preposterous lies meant to demean and degrade God's servants [1]. Moses warned that this rebellion was coming, saying, "I know thy rebellion, and thy stiff neck" (Deuteronomy 31:27) [3]. The books also note that rebels desire alternative leadership, defying and insulting their pastors and then seeking appointment under another man of God who does not even know them [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Those who are mad*, chapter 8 of *Those Who Rebel* and chapter 2 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 31:27-30; Joshua 22:19; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalms 139:21.

items.question: What is the difference between the true church and the false church?
items.text:
The true church, the bride of Christ, is always inviting people to God and saying, "Come to Jesus" [1]. The false church has no such message; instead it says, "Stay here! Settle down! Celebrate! Prosper today! Secure yourself! Enrich yourself! Make yourself happy!" [1].

The true church is evangelizing the world and saying to the whole world, "Come to God," while the false bride says, "Relax, take it easy, have fun, things are getting better for believers" [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *Make Yourselves Saviours of Men*.

items.question: Why is it so important for Christians to be part of a church assembly?
items.text:
The books speak to this warmly. The assembly is where your needs are met — material, emotional, marital, and family needs — and Scripture says of the early church that "neither was there any among them that lacked" (Acts 4:33-34) [1][3]. It is also a place of protection: wild animals survive by staying together, and it is the isolated buffalo that the lions pull down, so Satan is against the assembly because it prevents you from being isolated [2].

The assembly is where you are edified and built up in knowledge, understanding, morals, and faith (1 Corinthians 14:2-4) [6], and where revelation and knowledge are imparted (1 Corinthians 14:6) [1]. Healing power is present when we assemble, as when "the power of the Lord was present to heal them" (Luke 5:17) [2]. Coming together also produces unity — the more we come together, the more united we become [3] — and it keeps you from turning into a mocker, since it is those who separate themselves who become mockers (Jude 1:18-19) [3].

Practically, you must find a Bible-believing church and attend regularly, for "not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together" (Hebrews 10:25); like a coal separated from the fire, you cannot survive on your own, and "iron sharpeneth iron" (Proverbs 27:17) [4]. Jesus Himself had the habit of going to the synagogue as His custom (Luke 4:16) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 6 of *One Thousand Micro Churches* and chapter 10 of *Key Facts for New Believers*.

items.question: Why should I be a soul winner?
items.text:
You should be a soul winner because it is the great commission, the great command given to us by our Lord Jesus Christ, as Matthew 28:18-20 says [2]. It is also the very reason Jesus came to earth: "For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:10) [7]. Soul winning is the heartbeat of Jesus, and if we want to be Christ-like, we must be soul winners, since Christ Himself was one [3][7].

Beyond that, people are wasting their lives away without Jesus, and soul winning gives them a chance to become new creatures in Christ, as 2 Corinthians 5:17 says [1]. It also brings great joy and energizes Christians, for the seventy returned again with joy (Luke 10:1-3,17) [5]. And one day we will rejoice over the seeds we have sown, for "he that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing" (Psalm 126:6) [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Tell Them*.

items.question: Why does God allow my enemies to stay instead of removing them?
items.book: WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous
items.text:
The books give more than one answer to that, and I'll lay them out as they stand.

One reason is that God allows undefeated enemies to remain so His people can learn to fight and survive — He wants you to grow up and learn war, and He leaves some enemies so you have someone to spar with [1]. The Lord left those nations "only in order that the generations of the sons of Israel might be taught war," and to test Israel, to find out if they would obey His commandments (Judges 3:1-4) [1].

Another answer is that the fight is not over because God intends to destroy them. He has decided to destroy your enemies, and so He has caused them to harden their hearts, as Joshua 11:20 says, "The Lord had made them determined to fight the Israelites, so that they would be condemned to total destruction" [5]. The prolonging of the conflict is not because you are too weak; God wants it to carry on so He can use it as a basis to destroy them [5].

And a third: God uses your enemies for your good and promotion. Some of the greatest promotions come through enemies, and God used even Judas to bring about the greatest victory of Jesus' ministry [6]. As Psalm 119:71 says, "It is good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes" [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous* and chapters 7 and 15 of *TS2. Hope Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Joshua 11:20; Judges 2:21-3:4; Psalms 23:5; Psalms 119:71; John 12:24.

items.question: How can someone turn to God in a moment of complete desperation?
items.text:
When things go from bad to worse, that is supposed to turn you toward God — your problems are meant to bring you to Him, as the prodigal "came to himself" and said, "I will arise and go to my father" (Luke 15:17-18) [2]. It is time to repent and turn to God, returning to the Lord who tears and heals, who smites and binds up [2]. Repentance means turning around and going in the opposite direction, changing your mind and humbling yourself [2][8], and God commands all men everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30) [8].

Take heart that God is near to the brokenhearted: "The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit" (Psalm 34:18), and He is the God who comforts the depressed (2 Corinthians 7:6) [1]. He does not condemn you for speaking out your feelings in your desperation, and Jesus Himself was overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death as He prayed in Gethsemane [1]. In a crisis you can pray a short, powerful prayer and believe God has heard you, as Jesus did at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:41-42) [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 22 of *Those who are mad*, chapters 5 and 43 of *How You Can Preach Salvation* and chapter 6 of *100% Answered Prayer*.

In a crisis you can pray a short, powerful prayer and believe God has heard you, as Jesus did at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:41-42).

items.question: How can I tell if someone in my church is a false friend or a pretender?
items.text:
Friend, this is a burden many shepherds carry, and our books speak to it plainly. You are to watch for signs and symptoms, the way a doctor reads the body: notice people who are too quiet, for quiet people are dangerous and store up their thoughts within them [2]. Watch for those who seem to have two temperaments depending on who they are with, jovial with others but quiet and pensive in your presence [2]. Be careful, too, of those who are too perfect and dignified in their presentation, for that is often a façade for hidden things [2].

The clearest mark is the double picture: people who say nothing when they are in your presence but talk a lot when they are away from you [3][5]. A Judas is a liar who pretends to be telling the truth, a destroyer who pretends to be building, a covenant breaker who pretends to respect agreements, and one who cannot be trusted but pretends to be the most trustworthy person around [3]. So judge by actions and not by presentation, and prove all things, holding fast to that which is good, as 1 Thessalonians 5:20 says [2][3]. Do not be deceived by meek-faced people with sheepish grins who appear to admire your every decision [3][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Those Who Pretend, Intimidate And Are Familiar* and chapter 8 of *JUDAS
Who is he??*.

Scriptures referenced: Joshua 9:3-16; 1 Thessalonians 5:20.

items.question: What does the fear of man do to a person spiritually?
items.book: Demons and How to Deal with Them
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this. Fear is not merely a mood or an attitude — it is an evil spirit, and its presence is a sign of demonic activity [3][5]. When Adam rebelled, fear entered the human race for the first time, and rebels are full of fear and insecurity [1]. Fear takes away the soundness of your mind, so that you behave abnormally and cannot love as you should [2][3]. As 1 John 4:18 says, perfect love casts out fear, and the one who fears is not made perfect in love [7].

The books also warn that fear is a precursor to many evils — accusation, fault-finding, laziness, wickedness and poor performance — and that fearful people become suspicious, accusative, insecure, and can even become disloyal [4]. Fear destroys love and shows itself in suspicion and uncertainty [7]. And if you follow fear, you are following a demon, for God has not given us the spirit of fear [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Those Who Rebel*, chapter 4 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them*, chapter 26 of *Now We Are At War*, chapter 9 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies* and chapter 4 of *Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 3:9-10; Judges 7:3-4; Job 3:25; Psalms 34:4; Matthew 25:25; 2 Timothy 1:7; 1 John 4:18.

items.question: Can I still serve God while I'm busy with my studies or other responsibilities?
items.book: How you can become a strong Christian
items.text:
Yes, you can. The books say plainly that being a student is just another "care" of this world which must not be allowed to choke God's Word and work, and that God should not be excluded from your life because of your books [3][5]. One writer recalls that as a medical student he successfully combined his schoolwork with his pastoral work, being a student and a pastor for years, and says it is not an impossible task [3]. He even carried his seven-day-old son through cold weather and buses to keep a preaching appointment, saying, "My baby didn't die. Neither will yours, if you continue to do the work of the Lord" [5].

The warning is against letting those responsibilities dominate you. The thorns are the cares of the world which choke the word, and when they begin to dominate your life they kill your fruitfulness [3]. The demands of your job, the pressures of academic work, or bringing up little children can make you unfaithful, and if you are too busy to be involved in winning souls, then you are simply too busy [4]. So rise up and be fruitful in spite of all the cares and responsibilities of the world [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 3 of *Bearing Fruit After Your Kind*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 22:13; Mark 4:19.

items.question: How do I become a better leader of people?
items.text:
The books say a good leader works on the people he leads until they become better human beings, not just carrying a title [1]. Jesus spent three years with His disciples and their lives were completely transformed, so that people marveled at their boldness and knew they had been with Jesus (Acts 4:13) [1]. A leader also reproduces himself in others, preparing them for the day he is no longer around, as Jesus did with His disciples (John 16:4-5) [3].

Practically, the books urge you to value people, since people are drawn to places where they are valued and every person who feels undervalued will move away [7]. They also call you to be at peace with those around you and to bring peace between people, following peace with all men (Hebrews 12:14) [2]. And they say to listen to people's problems, let conversations center on others rather than yourself, encourage, say thank you, smile, and avoid partiality, for the wisdom from above is without partiality (James 3:17) [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 20, 23, 86, 121 and 126 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Ruth 4:15; 1 Samuel 1:8; 2 Samuel 18:3; John 16:4-5; John 16:16; John 16:23; Acts 4:13; Philippians 1:19; 2 Timothy 2:1; Philemon 19 and 1 more.

items.question: How can a pastor grow an empty church?
items.text:
Friend, our books speak to this. A pastor without anagkazo will have an empty church, and without it many churches will die a natural death; you must go out and compel people to come in, rather than sitting in church and inviting them [1]. The people who will fill empty churches are not in places where they receive polite invitation cards, so a new strategy of going to the gutters, highways and the bushes must be employed [1].

But growth also begins inside you: in the absence of a burning vision for a large church you will never have real church growth, and that burning vision is the invisible engine that drives a minister from a small church to a mega church [6][8]. Attempt great things for God — attempt to grow a church, for your church can grow if the Holy Spirit is working through you, and you are destined to multiply (Jeremiah 30:19) [2]. Also spend your time with the twenty percent who bring the increase, for eighty percent of church growth comes from twenty percent of your members [5]. And be aware that some barrenness is spiritual: one church could not grow until a demon above the congregation was dealt with, and another until an evil spirit in the ceiling was rebuked [3][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1 and 27 of *Church Growth*, chapter 11 of *Attempt Great Things for God*, chapter 11 of *Church Planting*, chapter 9 of *One of You is a Devil* and chapter 13 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 29:18; Proverbs 30:16; Jeremiah 17:6; Jeremiah 30:19; Matthew 16:23; Acts 16:5.

items.question: How can I learn to work with different kinds of people to accomplish what God has called me to do?
items.book: What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent
items.text:
Friend, this is a good and needed question, and our books speak to it directly.

The heart of it is that your calling grows as your circle of people grows. Nehemiah worked with forty-one different kinds of people, and the number of different groups you can work with reveals the magnitude of your calling [1]. So aspire to have that grace to work with all kinds of people, since Jesus came to die for all kindred, nations, tribes and tongues [1]. Peter had to learn this too, when God showed him he should not call any man common or unclean (Acts 10:28), and Paul said he became all things to all men that he might by all means save some (1 Corinthians 9:22,23) [5].

Practically, the books name specific people you must learn to work with: your own church members, whom a pastor must both understand and discipline [2]; unbelievers whose expertise you need, for some die-hard sinners you will have to engage if you are to succeed [2]; people older than you, with carefulness and respect [2]; and volunteers you do not pay, for people feel happy when given a little task [2][4]. Also women, without falling into sin or quarrelling [4]; people who do not like each other but must work together, as Paul urged Euodias and Syntyche to be of the same mind in the Lord (Philippians 4:2) [4]; and technical people, by knowing a little about everything and asking many questions [4].

And remember, your limitations are overcome by recognizing the contribution of others, for every joint supplies something until you become what God has called you to be (Ephesians 4:16) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *The Art of Following*, chapter 22 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*, chapter 100 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 6 of *Many Are Called*.

Scriptures referenced: Acts 10:28; 1 Corinthians 9:22-23; Ephesians 4:16; Philippians 4:2.

items.question: Can my friends keep me from staying close to God?
items.text:
Yes, friends can affect your closeness to God, though the books put the responsibility on you. They warn that "they that are far from thee shall perish," and that closeness is a test of your survival, so you must fight to be close to God and to those who matter in your life [3]. The same passage tells you to learn from close people, to watch what they do to come close, and not to be one of the distant people who only say "hi" and "bye" [3].

But the books also say that nearness is not physical — someone sitting six thousand miles away may be closer than you sitting at his feet [1]. And they say it is up to you to draw near: "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you" (James 4:8) [7]. So the deciding factor is not who is around you but whether you keep going to Him.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 16 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them*, chapter 6 of *WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous* and chapter 5 of *The Secret*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 65:4; Psalms 73:27-28; Mark 12:34; James 4:8.

items.question: How can they come back?
items.text:
The books describe the way back mainly as repentance and returning to God. Jeremiah repeatedly urged the people, "Turn away from your wicked ways. Stop doing evil! Repent and come back to God" [2]. God also invites the backslider to reason with Him, saying, "Come now, and let us reason together" (Isaiah 1:18) [3].

Beyond that, the books point to prayer as strength against falling: Jesus told His disciples to pray because they might fall into temptation, and a Christian who doesn't pray will fall into one temptation after another [7]. They also stress being planted and committed in a church, like a tree by the rivers of water, with a pastor to relate to, since God made us like sheep who need a shepherd [7]. And they call believers to adapt to new circumstances rather than turn their backs on God because of them, singing the Lord's song wherever they find themselves (Psalm 137:4; Psalm 118:14) [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 7 and 8 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 118:14; Psalms 137:4; Proverbs 7:10; Isaiah 1:18.

items.question: Why do people who speak against God seem to prosper?
items.text:
Our books speak to this. One reason is that such prospering is itself determined by God: those who speak marvellous things against the God of gods "shall prosper till the indignation be accomplished: for that that is determined shall be done" (Daniel 11:35-36) [1]. Even the threats and attacks gathered against Jesus were "to do whatever your hand and your purpose predestined to occur" [1]. And the beast was given "a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies," with power to continue forty-two months — after which blasphemies were no longer allowed (Revelation 13:4-7) [6].

Another reason is that God often allows people to stray into His imperfect will and then receive a fitting judgment later. Many sins are allowed to continue for years until the cup is full; the children of Israel had to murmur ten times before God reacted [8]. So do not be put off by blasphemies and injurious speech levelled against God's man of faith and power [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Predestination*, chapter 8 of *Those Who Are Offended* and chapter 26 of *Why Few Are Chosen*.

Scriptures referenced: Daniel 11:35-36; Romans 13:1; Revelation 13:4-7.

items.question: How do I deal with disloyal people?
items.text:
The books speak plainly to this. Teaching the Word of God regularly is the preventive way to deal with disloyalty, because teaching fights deception, and it is only deceived people who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer [3]. When disloyalty is already present, the biblical remedy for a scorner is to cast him out — to dismiss, expel, eject, banish, fire, sack, discard, unseat or lay off — as Proverbs 22:10 says, "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out" [5]. You must also wipe out the associates of disloyal people, letting them go openly to the camp they love, since God cast out Lucifer and the angels associated with him (Revelation 12:9) [1].

You must be fierce and resolute, not dealing with the enemy in a spirit of benevolence, for all forms of disloyalty will end a church and a ministry [4]. Handle them God's way, with knowledge and wisdom, binding and restricting a "Judas" rather than letting him operate freely [7]. Dismiss disloyal and offending workers completely, even longstanding ones, while in mercy making financial provision so they can live and work elsewhere — this prevents the root of bitterness from spreading, as Hebrews 12:15 warns [8].

items.question: How can I escape the curse on this earth and start living in God's blessings instead?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this directly, and the answer they give is wisdom from above. God's wisdom from above is the master key to overcoming the curse on this earth, and anything in the Word of God is that wisdom — following any aspect of it will lift you above the curse [1][3]. So seek the kingdom of God first, and the supernatural power of God is released to make you prosper, as Matthew 6:33 says [3]. When you work for God, the curse that is in the ground is avoided, because you are not tilling the ground for bread but working in His vineyard, and those who obey and serve Him are promised to spend their days in prosperity, as Job 36:11 says [3].

The books also point to the anointing: the yoke shall be destroyed because of the anointing, as Isaiah 10:27 says, and the master key to exiting a cursed path is to follow the direction of the Holy Spirit and listen to the voice of God [4][6]. As many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God (Romans 8:14), so being led by Him lifts you out of a cursed existence into a supernatural one [3]. And seek the blessings themselves, for through a blessing you can counteract a curse no matter how strong it is — life and death, blessing and cursing are set before you, so choose life, as Deuteronomy 30:19 says [5][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 23, 24 and 31 of *How To Neutralize Curses*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 1:28; Genesis 3:19; Genesis 9:1; Deuteronomy 28:1; Deuteronomy 30:19; Job 36:11; Isaiah 10:27; Daniel 5:11-12; Matthew 6:33; Romans 8:14 and 1 more.

items.question: How can a young leader make up for not having much experience?
items.text:
The books speak directly to this. A young leader makes up for inexperience by studying history: "The most important subject for a young leader is history," because a young person has to tap into the experiences of others, and his only chance of avoiding certain mistakes is to study those who went before him [1]. History is the greatest source of knowledge and wisdom, second only to the Scriptures, and the Scriptures themselves contain many history lessons that guide us [1]. As Ecclesiastes 1:9,10 says, there is no new thing under the sun [1].

The books also say experience itself is a teacher: there are many things that can only be learned by experience, and the Father even trained Jesus this way, for as Hebrews 5:8 says, He learned obedience through the things He suffered [7]. And an experienced person is someone who knows the difference between the ideal and the real, so do not despise the lessons of maturity you are learning [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 35, 40 and 124 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Ecclesiastes 1:9-10; Hebrews 5:8.

items.question: Can I get to heaven after I die if I know the right people?
items.book: How to be Born again & Avoid Hell
items.text:
No, friend. When you die you will discover that there is a big gap between heaven and hell, and people cannot cross over from hell to heaven no matter who they are and no matter how much money they had on earth [1][2]. If you want to cross, you must cross now, because you cannot transfer when you die [1][2]. As Luke 16:26 says, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed, so that none can pass from one side to the other [1][2].

Salvation will be through the blood of Jesus and not through "whom you know" [1][2]. Jesus said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" (John 14:6) [4], and unless a man is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God (John 3:3) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 20 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*, chapter 4 of *How to be Born again & Avoid Hell* and chapter 16 of *People Who Went to Hell*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 5:13-14; Luke 16:25-26; John 3:3; John 14:6.

items.question: Why do people leave the church over small offenses?
items.text:
People often leave a church not because of doctrine but because of unresolved hurts. One pastor found that a man who claimed the Spirit led him to leave had actually been wounded, and "his unresolved hurts had caused him to be cut off from his church," which is "one of the commonest reasons for people backsliding and leaving churches" [8].

Sometimes what looks like a small offense is really a cover for something else. In one account, a man complained that his pastor's sermons were not uplifting, but he was actually having an affair and "didn't like his sin being exposed" — such Christians "can easily leave church to avoid the confrontations of God's Word, instead of admitting their sins and repenting" [3]. And some leave out of selfishness, having "drunk from the pulpit of a church for several years," then causing a stir and damaging the church's reputation on the way out [2][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Those who leave you*, chapter 3 of *Backsliding* and chapter 7 of *Opportunities*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 1:10; Ezekiel 34:18.

items.question: What does it mean that Jesus is a warrior king and we fight alongside him?
items.text:
Yes, that is exactly the picture our books paint. Jesus Himself leads the armies of Heaven and makes war in righteousness, and the armies of Heaven follow Him on white horses, clothed in fine linen, white and clean [1][2]. He is the Lamb who makes war and overcomes the kings who unite against Him, for He is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with Him are called, chosen, and faithful [2][4].

So if you want to follow Jesus, you have to join His army and you have to fight [2][6]. God Himself teaches our hands to war (Psalm 18:34), and we are instructed to fight the good fight of faith (1 Timothy 6:12) and to war a good warfare (1 Timothy 1:18) [4]. Anyone who thinks we are not at war lacks understanding; God wants us to wage war in His way and in His wisdom, in righteousness [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in *Now We Are At War* and page 1 of *A Good General*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 18:34; 1 Timothy 1:18; 1 Timothy 6:12; Revelation 17:12-14; Revelation 19:11-16.

items.question: How can I make my faith stronger?
items.book: Name It Claim It Take It
items.text:
What a good question to ask, pastor. Our books say the principal way to improve your faith is by hearing: "faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God" (Romans 10:17) [2]. The more you listen to preaching and teaching, the more your faith is built up, so keep listening to messages you love over and over, old ones and new, and read the books God has placed in your hands [5][8]. Watching Christian preaching videos will increase your faith too, and you can listen while walking and while working [5].

Faith also grows when you use it; the scripture teaches that we gain by using what we have (Luke 19:15) [5]. So grow in faith and believe God for bigger things [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Name It Claim It Take It* and chapters 14 and 68 of *Faith Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 47:9; Luke 19:15; Romans 10:17; 2 Thessalonians 1:3.

items.question: How do we know the Bible is really God's Word and not just written by men?
items.text:
What a good question to ask, and our books speak to it plainly. The Bible's own claim is that it did not come by man's will: "no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost" (2 Peter 1:20, 21) [3]. It was written by honest and godly men, and we can tell because it condemns all sin and even records the sins and faults of its own writers — something evil men would not do, and good men would not do unless inspired to help others [1]. As 2 Timothy 3:16 says, "All scripture is given by inspiration of God" [2][4][8].

The books also point to evidence beyond the claim itself. The Bible has been preserved through the ages — whole kingdoms and religions have sought in vain to destroy it, and God has made it indestructible and victorious [1]. Its heavenly and eternal contents prove it to be of God [1], and the wisest, most godly and honest men acknowledge it as the Word of God, while only infidels and ungodly people reject it [1]. Even great men have testified to it — Woodrow Wilson said you will know the Bible is the Word of God when you read it, for in it you will find the key to your own heart, your own happiness, and your success [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 7 and 8 of *Read your Bible Pray Everyday*, chapter 7 of *Key Facts for New Believers* and chapter 8 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 119:9; Psalms 119:105; Acts 20:32; Romans 1:16; 1 Corinthians 2:14; 2 Timothy 3:16-17; Hebrews 1:1-2; Hebrews 2:1-4; 2 Peter 1:20-21.

items.question: What does the Bible say will happen to people who gossip and slander others in the church?
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this, and it is a sobering picture. A slanderer is due a curse, and "may a slanderer not endure on the earth; may evil hunt a violent person violently" (Psalm 140:11) — their stay on earth is cut short, and they must watch over their shoulders constantly [1]. The end of all blasphemers and disloyal people will be fire, brimstone, cursing, vexation and desolation of long continuance, for slanderers are cursed men [5].

There is also a word about the church itself. Psalm 15:1-3 describes who may reside in God's tent and settle on His holy hill — one who does not slander with his tongue — so once you have slandered the brethren, you can no longer be allowed to stay and dwell amongst us [1]. And the Lord says, "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people" (Leviticus 19:16), for it is a sin to be an active campaigner and spreader of lies and scandalous stories [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 9 of *Those Who Are Slanderers* and chapter 9 of *Pillars of Loyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 19:16; Psalms 15:1-5; Psalms 105:15; Psalms 140:11; Revelation 13:4-7.

items.question: How can I receive a share of the Holy Spirit's anointing like the seventy elders did with Moses?
items.text:
The Scriptures in our books show that the anointing is shared by God Himself, not engineered by us. It was God who took of the spirit that was upon Moses and put it upon the seventy elders — Moses did not transfer it, and the elders did not take it for themselves [3]. As John 3:27 says, a man can receive nothing except it be given him from heaven [3].

That said, God has chosen to place His mantle on human beings, and He often directs you to an anointed person [5]. If you involve yourself and join yourself with people who are anointed, you can merge into the anointing they carry, as Elisha bonded himself to Elijah [2]. So respect anointed men, because they carry the anointing you desire, and handle them carefully — many who quarrel with their spiritual fathers never receive what they seek [5]. And follow the Lord faithfully for several years, as everyone in the upper room had done before they were filled with the Holy Ghost [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Tasters And Partakers*, chapter 10 of *The Anointed and His Anointing* and chapter 8 of *Steps to the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 11:16-17; Numbers 11:24-25; John 3:27; Acts 1:8; Acts 1:21-23; Acts 2:4.

items.question: Why did the people on Malta first think Paul was a murderer and then change their minds to think he was a god?
items.text:
When Paul was gathering sticks for the fire, a viper fastened on his hand, and the barbarians said among themselves, "No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he hath escaped the sea, yet vengeance suffereth not to live" [2][4]. They expected him to swell up or fall down dead suddenly, but after they had looked a great while and saw no harm come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god [2][3][6].

That shift shows how much honour has to do with the way you think about a person; negative thoughts are a clear sign of the absence of honour [1]. Later, when Paul prayed and laid hands on Publius' father and healed him, and others on the island with diseases came and were healed, the people honoured them with many honours and loaded them with such things as were necessary (Acts 28:1-10) [4][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 4 and 8 of *Those Who Honour You*, chapter 11 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church* and chapter 53 of *The Gift Of Governments*.

Scriptures referenced: Malachi 1:6-8; Acts 27:41-28:10.

items.question: Does sleeping too much really lead to poverty?
items.text:
Yes, our books speak to this plainly. Too much sleep and too much rest lead to poverty: "Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man" (Proverbs 6:9-11) [1]. Poverty comes like a traveller you cannot send away, and want like an armed man you cannot easily dismiss [1]. The same lesson is drawn from the field of the sluggard, overgrown with thorns and nettles (Proverbs 24:30-34) [2][3][4][5].

King Solomon analysed poverty around him and concluded that much of it was caused by lack of hard work — that if sleep and folding of arms were dealt with, there would be more prosperity [4]. One book adds the caution that not all poor people are lazy, but notes that some stay in poverty because they do not want to work hard [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Awake, O Sleeper*, chapter 9 of *Why Is This Church Not Working?*, chapter 85 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 11 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 6:9-11; Proverbs 24:30-34.

items.question: A teenager in our youth group says he cuts himself when he is sad.
items.text:
I'm so glad you're carrying this with you, pastor. Our books speak directly to this. The madman of Gadara, fully under the influence of Satan, cut himself with stones — and this is described as a very important manifestation of the presence of Satan: self-destruction [8]. The demonized man of Gadara tried to kill himself by cutting himself with stones [1]. Self-destruction is one of the key strategies of demonic attacks; when the spirit of Satan takes hold of a person, he will often begin to cut himself with stones [2].

The books also say that what makes people so sad that they give up on life and become suicidal can only be demons [3], and that demons make people suicidal and tell them to destroy themselves and end their lives [5]. They note that suicide is a common symptom of depression and can occur in other mental conditions such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder [5], and that people with depression are suicidal [6]. The books also say that many medical mental health conditions lead to suicide, and that depression patients are prone to committing suicide [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 7, 14 and 22 of *Those who are mad* and chapters 9 and 11 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 19:16; 1 Kings 19:2-4; Isaiah 61:3; Ezekiel 28:16-18; Jonah 4:1-9; Mark 5:5; John 16:2; Romans 16:17.

items.question: How can wisdom help me when I'm facing a situation that seems impossible?
items.text:
Wisdom is the application of God's word to impossible situations, and it gives you grace to overcome where others would have drowned [1]. The poor wise man in the besieged city delivered it by wisdom, not by strength, and Scripture says "wisdom is better than strength" (Ecclesiastes 9:14-16) [1][5]. So when you face something with no way out, wisdom is the key that solves impossible situations [4][5].

That wisdom is available to you. It comes through reading—take the books of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes and ask God for wisdom for the affairs of life [8]—and through prayer, for "if any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally" (James 1:5) [8]. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of wisdom, and through wisdom you can overcome impossible situations [3][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*, chapter 21 of *Attempt Great Things for God*, chapters 12 and 19 of *Daughter, You Can Make It* and chapter 84 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 4:7-8; Ecclesiastes 9:14-16; Ecclesiastes 10:10; 1 Corinthians 1:24; James 1:5; Wisdom of Solomon 1:1-77.

items.question: How do I understand when Jesus says we must hate our father and mother to be His disciple?
items.text:
That is a hard saying, and our books treat it as exactly that — a saying too deep for most of us, one you may not be meant to understand but to obey if and when such a day dawns on your life [1]. Jesus said plainly, "If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple" (Luke 14:26), and the books read this as a real time and place where hatred for father, mother, wife and children becomes a necessary qualification to be His disciple [2]. It seems to contradict the Word that teaches us to honour our fathers and mothers, and to love our wives — and the books do not explain that tension away [1][2].

One thing they do say is that this is a teaching reserved for those called at a higher level, applicable to people who may have to hate their wives in order to fulfil their divine calling — the kind of thing Jesus gave privately to His disciples rather than to the congregation [3]. And it is not a licence for sin: the book is meant to bring you closer to God, not to be an excuse to do bad things [2]. As for how to grasp it, the counsel is to travel with the anointed, for there are things Jesus hid from the public and revealed only when moving privately with His disciples (Matthew 13:10-11) [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *The Tree and Your Ministry* and chapter 20 of *The Anointed and His Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 2:9; Matthew 13:10-11; Luke 14:26.

items.question: Why doesn't God answer some of my prayers?
items.text:
I hear the ache in that question, and our books speak to it in a few ways.

Sometimes the answer is no because what we ask is impossible for Him to do — God will have to say "no" when we ask Him for things which are impossible for Him to do [1][2]. And sin matters: our iniquities have made a separation between us and God, and our sins have hidden His face so that He does not hear (Isaiah 59:1-2) [5]. The books also say plainly that God does not answer the prayers of disobedient children, while the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much (James 5:16) [7].

There is another side too. Jesus prayed for only one sick man though hundreds needed help, because He did what He saw the Father doing (John 5:19) — He would not get involved in things God was not actively doing [1][2]. One book says it may be God's will to heal everybody, and perhaps it was simply not yet time for certain healings to manifest [1]; another says it may not be God's will to heal everybody, and perhaps the circumstances of each illness differed [2]. Both are held out to you.

And our books admit mystery here: God seems to want us to keep asking about the same things even though we have asked before, and it is not easy to solve why some prayers are repetitious to Him and some are not [8]. So keep praying — He is alive and hears, and He wants to bless you [4][6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 9 of *How to Pray*, chapters 1 and 5 of *100% Answered Prayer* and chapter 110 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 59:1-2; Matthew 6:7-8; John 5:1-8; John 5:19; John 15:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:17; James 5:16.

items.question: How can I receive an impartation of understanding from the Holy Spirit?
items.text:
Friend, our books speak to this. The Holy Spirit is the spirit of understanding, and a sudden great illumination of understanding, knowledge or revelation should alert you to an impartation [1]. That impartation often comes as you hear the anointed: the spirit entered into Ezekiel when he spoke to him (Ezekiel 2:2), and the household of Cornelius received the anointing while Peter was still speaking (Acts 10:44) [2]. So present your heart as a tablet, expecting not only insight but the impartation that makes the insight produce, for holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Ghost [4].

Keep listening with faith, even to what you do not yet understand; you receive the Spirit by the hearing of faith (Galatians 3:2) [5][8]. Soak in a series of messages until you are saturated, and listen more than once [8]. And pray for the Holy Spirit, for He is given to those who ask (Luke 11:13) [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *The Anointed and His Anointing*, chapter 31 of *The Sweet Influences of the Anointing*, chapter 8 of *Catch The Anointing* and chapter 13 of *Seeing And Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 11:1; Isaiah 34:16; Ezekiel 2:2; Luke 11:13; Acts 10:44; Galatians 3:2; 1 Timothy 5:22.

items.question: What happens if I don't forgive someone?
items.text:
If you don't forgive, the books say the consequences are serious. God will not forgive your sins and will not hear your prayers [1][2][6], and the devil will torment you—with sickness, disease, poverty, or marital disharmony—even if powerful men of God lay hands on you [2]. God will be angry with you because He forgave you but you would not forgive others, and you may be handed over to the tormentors [1]. As Mark 11:25 says, when you stand praying, forgive, so that your Father in heaven may forgive your trespasses [6]. The books even say unforgiveness is one sin God will not forgive, and it may be for you the difference between life and death [6].

There is also a picture of what unforgiveness does over time: hurt can degenerate into bitterness, spreading from one offender to hatred of many, and bitterness poisons others when a bitter person speaks [7]. And it can isolate you—people who are hurt withdraw and live alone, while forgiveness is what builds a large family [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 4, 5 and 7 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 46:26-27; Genesis 48:20-22; Psalms 130:4; Jeremiah 17:9; Matthew 18:32-35; Mark 11:25.

items.question: What is blasphemy?
items.text:
Blasphemy is speaking reproachfully about God and His work — speaking evil in a way that incurs God's wrath, and speaking impiously or maliciously against God, His church, and His servants [1]. It is also defined as an act of cursing or reviling God, and as vilification, slander, and injurious speech against another's good name [2][3]. It includes speaking irreverently about sacred things, and ministers are in a certain sense sacred because they have been set apart to minister the holy things of the Lord [6].

The books also say disloyalty is equated to blasphemy, so that anyone who blasphemes is being disloyal and anyone who is disloyal is a blasphemer [2]. And it warns that born-again Christians can make this mistake too — whenever you accuse a minister of being a false prophet, deceiver, anointed of the devil, or the like, you could be blaspheming [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Those Who Make Shipwreck*, chapter 9 of *Pillars of Loyalty*, chapter 16 of *Victory Secrets* and chapter 6 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue*.

Scriptures referenced: Mark 3:28-30; Revelation 2:9; Revelation 13:4-7.

items.question: How does the blood of Jesus cleanse me from my sins?
items.text:
Friend, the books say plainly that nothing else can wash away the stain of sin — not soaps or detergents, and not orange juice or apple juice either. Only the blood of Jesus has the power to wash away our lies, our stealing, our fornication and our murders [1][2][6]. As 1 John 1:7 puts it, the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin [3][4][7].

They also describe it as a cleansing that goes one step further than forgiveness. You may be forgiven, yet there is often a scent of the past evils that contaminate us, so after being forgiven you need cleansing [4][6][8]. The picture given is of a man pulled from a septic tank: his life was saved, but he still smelled bad and needed a thorough bath [4][6][8]. And the blood keeps cleansing regularly, carrying away our sin and filthiness as we walk in the light and confess our sins, for he is faithful and just to forgive us and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 12, 14, 16 and 46 of *How You Can Preach Salvation* and chapters 3, 5 and 6 of *Blood Power*.

Scriptures referenced: Zechariah 3:3-4; John 6:54-55; Acts 4:12; 1 John 1:7; 1 John 1:9; Revelation 1:5; Revelation 22:11.

items.question: Does God want me to fight spiritual battles, and how do I do that?
items.text:
Yes, dear pastor, the books are clear that God does want you to fight. Jesus Christ leads the armies of heaven and makes war in righteousness (Revelation 19:11), and if you want to follow Jesus, you have to join His army and fight [3]. You are told to "fight the good fight of faith" (1 Timothy 6:12), and to prepare yourself to fight even more because you are a minister of the gospel [4].

As for how, you must accept that you will build for God and fight battles at the same time — that is part of the call, especially in this end time [1]. You will fight battles outside and within, physical beings and spiritual beings, enemies who look like enemies and enemies who look like friends [1]. So put on the whole armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil (Ephesians 6:11), for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds (2 Corinthians 10:4) [6]. And remember that your principal enemy is Satan and not other human beings [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *The Art of Following*, chapters 1, 3 and 60 of *A Good General* and chapter 4 of *Transform Your Pastoral Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Nehemiah 4:17-18; 1 Corinthians 14:10; 2 Corinthians 10:4; Ephesians 6:10-11; 1 Timothy 6:12; Revelation 19:11; Revelation 20:1-3; Revelation 20:10.

items.question: Do pastors and church workers have the right to be paid and take time off?
items.book: Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)
items.text:
Yes, dear pastor, the books speak plainly to both. On pay: a full-time church worker should be considered for emoluments, benefits, accommodation, transportation, medical care, insurance, emergencies, compassionate donations and love offerings when the organisation is capable of doing so [4]. The Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel, as 1 Corinthians 9:14 says [8], and the husbandman that laboureth must be first partaker of the fruits, as 2 Timothy 2:6 says [8]. Paul asks whether a soldier pays his own expenses, or a farmer eats no part of his crop, or a shepherd drinks no milk [2], and God's law said not to muzzle the ox treading out the wheat [2].

On rest: rest is part of God's plan for His cherished ministers, and God wants full-time ministers to have vacations, days off and times of rest — it is their right [1]. Paul asked, "Or do only Barnabas and I not have a right to refrain from working?" (1 Corinthians 9:6) [1]. Full-time church workers should also have rest and leave periods, of various kinds, created and determined by the administrators and bishops in their various denominations and churches [3][4]. Mondays can be taken as a day of rest and a day off [3]. One caution from the books: in emergency situations affecting the church or the nation, all full-time church workers must cancel vacations and return to work [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)*, chapter 55 of *The Gift Of Governments* and chapter 38 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:22-23; Ecclesiastes 10:7; 1 Corinthians 9:4; 1 Corinthians 9:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14; 1 Timothy 4:15; 2 Timothy 2:6.

items.question: How do I heal from the hurts and offenses I've experienced in life and ministry?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak directly to this, and they speak tenderly. First, expect to be hurt — it is part of this life and especially of ministry. "If you are in the ministry, expect to be hurt and wounded by fellow pastors" [2], and Jesus Himself said offences must come (Matthew 18:6-7) [2][5]. So your wounds do not mean something has gone wrong with you.

The healing itself comes through confession and prayer: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed" (James 5:16) [2][5]. You are healed when you are no longer bitter, and you are meant to come out of the trial with patience — cheerful, hopeful endurance (James 1:4) [2]. The Lord Himself was anointed "to heal the broken hearted" (Luke 4:18-19) [2], and He will heal you of your wounds [5]. Do not let the offence isolate you; withdrawing from other Christians in the name of caution leads to isolation and backsliding [1][3]. And as you heal, hold on to Romans 8:28 — all things work together for good to them that love the Lord [4]; your healed wounds become scars that give you authority and a healing ministry [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapter 17 of *TS2. Hope Secrets*, chapter 3 of *Backsliding* and chapter 9 of *Those Who Are Offended*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 18:6-7; Luke 4:18-19; Romans 8:28; James 1:4; James 5:16.

items.question: How should an assistant minister behave during counselling sessions with the senior pastor?
items.text:
During counselling sessions, you should assist properly: don't contribute any counsel that is contrary to what is being said, and don't try to develop a completely new train of thought, which may only confuse the one receiving counsel [1][2]. Don't try to impress anyone with "high-sounding" wisdom; simply help your senior say what he is saying better and emphasize what he has already said [1][2]. Do not remain quiet, though, for that makes you look like a spectator and makes the counsellee feel awkward [1][2].

You can use simple phrases at intervals, such as "Do you understand what Pastor is saying?", "Do you understand that Pastor is only trying to help you?", "Pastor is only saying this because he loves you," and "I wish I had had someone speak to me this way when I was in a similar situation" [2][3]. As you interject comments like these, you lend a greater impact to his words [2][3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapter 3 of *Ministerial Ethics*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 18:16.

items.question: What should I do if I'm bitter about being moved away from a pastor who helped me?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this. Our books speak to this, and gently.

Bitterness is an advanced, deep-seated form of offense, and many who walk out of a church are offended Christians who became bitter, with wounds that never healed [2]. The answer is forgiveness: as Mark 11:25 says, when you stand praying, forgive if you have anything against any, so that your Father in heaven may forgive you your trespasses [8]. As you forgive, you are liberated from bitterness and can begin to experience joy again, and you can ask the Holy Spirit to help you [8]. It also helps to talk about your pain with spiritually mature counsellors, pastors, or godly friends, and to confess your faults one to another and pray for one another that you may be healed, as James 5:16 says — though after a while you must consciously stop talking about your pain, or you will wear your counsellors out and not make much progress [8].

One caution from the books: do not let the rest of your ministry be coloured by mistrust, because a lack of trust reveals continuing bitterness in you, and Hebrews 12:15 warns lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you and thereby many be defiled [3]. And do not be moved by a change in your circumstances, for as Acts 2:25 says, the Lord is always before your face, that you should not be moved [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapter 10 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 59 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 103:8; Mark 11:24-25; Acts 2:25; Hebrews 12:15; James 5:16.

items.question: How does prayer make me stronger?
items.text:
Prayer is where your strength comes from, pastor. When you cry out to God, He answers and strengthens you with strength in your soul (Psalm 138:3) [2]. That strength is what you need for ministry, for surviving the attacks of the enemy, and for emotional steadiness, since your soul is your emotions, will, and intellect [2].

It also works in very practical ways. Praying in tongues builds you up and makes you stronger, for "he that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself" (1 Corinthians 14:4) [1]. Angels can bring you strength in prayer, as one appeared to Jesus in His agony and strengthened Him (Luke 22:41-43) [1]. And prayer strengthens your spirit so your weak flesh is controlled, since the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak (Matthew 26:41) [3][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 12 and 14 of *Pr 6. Prayer Opportunities*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 138:3; Matthew 26:41; Luke 22:41-43; 1 Corinthians 14:4; Ephesians 3:14-19; 1 Timothy 1:12; 2 Timothy 1:6-7; 2 Timothy 4:17.

Attacks that involve stealing, killing and destruction are caused by the devil and his agents, and spending time to bind demonic powers and destroy their plans will protect you from such evil attacks [1]. Persistent attacks are a sign of demonic activity — Job experienced persistent attacks on his family, his life and his health, and those events were the result of Satan's direct attack on him, as Job 1:12 shows [5]. Demons and demonic activity must be identified in order to be dealt with, so begin to mention the names of the spirits harassing you and ask God to reveal the real identity of the spirits [4]. You can also tighten your security: staying with the truth and avoiding deception, and practicing righteousness and avoiding sin, tighten the security of your spirit man against demons, as Ephesians 6:14 says [7].

items.question: Can someone who gossips or slanders others still be a member of our church?
items.text:
Our books speak plainly to this. A slanderer will not be allowed to remain in the church: Psalm 15 describes those who may dwell in God's holy hill, and it says the one who does not slander with his tongue is the one who may stay [1]. Once you have slandered the brethren, you can no longer be allowed to stay and dwell amongst us [1][2]. So no slanderer can be allowed to settle in amongst us; drive them away and let them go [2].

The same books also say a slanderer is somebody who must be driven away from the church, along with the double-tongued, the murmurer, the evil critic, and the talebearer [5]. And be careful not to receive people who come with stories and rumours against their former church or employer, for that is the same spirit [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *Those Who Are Slanderers* and chapter 11 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

items.question: Why is loyalty so important in ministry, especially during hard times?
items.text:
Loyalty matters because it is the principal qualification for every minister — "it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful" (1 Corinthians 4:2) [3][7]. It is not gifting, friendliness, or oratory that qualifies a person, but faithfulness, dependability, and constancy [7].

Hard times are where loyalty shows its true worth. In the good times everybody seems loyal, but loyalty is most appreciated in hard times [1][2]. Jesus told His disciples they would receive a special reward because they had continued with Him in His temptations (Luke 22:28-29), and their names are written on the foundations of the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:14) [1][2]. Those who stick with you through difficult times are different from those who come in when everything is working well [2][4].

Loyalty also brings life and growth: pursuing loyalty leads to life, righteousness, and honour (Proverbs 21:21), and the blessing of largeness is reserved for faithful and loyal people [5][6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 7 of *Why Loyalty?*, chapters 1 and 12 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapter 2 of *Pillars of Loyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 21:21; Ecclesiastes 12:12; Matthew 25:21; Luke 22:28-29; 1 Corinthians 4:2; Revelation 21:14.

items.question: How does the Holy Spirit teach us today?
items.text:
The Holy Spirit teaches us first and foremost as a teacher — that is His number one manifestation, and He makes Himself visible and relevant to us by teaching us all things [3]. Jesus promised that the Comforter would teach us all things and bring all things to our remembrance, whatsoever He had said unto us (John 14:26) [1][3][5][8]. So when you read your Bible and begin to have deep revelations of the Word, the Holy Spirit is being manifest [3].

He teaches in several ways. He guides us into all truth, for He shall not speak of Himself, but whatsoever He shall hear, that shall He speak, and He will show us things to come (John 16:12–13) [1][5][7]. He teaches through revelation — the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Him (Ephesians 1:17) [1]. He reminds us of things, and you do not know the Holy Spirit if you do not know Him as a "reminder" [1][5][8]. He points you toward certain books you must read [5]. And He gives teachers — He will speak to you through people anointed to teach the word of God, so do not miss the voice of the Holy Spirit that comes to you through an anointed teacher of the Word [5]. He may speak to your spirit, soul, or body, and His voice to your spirit is called the "inner witness" [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *The Love of the Spirit*, chapter 7 of *Amplify Your Ministry with Miracles And Manifestations Of The Holy Spirit* and chapter 10 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Nehemiah 9:20; John 14:26; John 16:12-14; Ephesians 1:17; 2 Peter 1:3; Revelation 10:8.

items.question: How can I tell when someone in my team is becoming disloyal?
items.text:
Friend, the books say disloyalty doesn't happen overnight — becoming disloyal is a process, and most people don't even notice it in themselves or in those they work with [1]. The first stage is an independent spirit: the person is still part of the church but does what he wants in spite of contrary instructions, obeying only the instructions he thinks are really important [1].

Watch too for the signs: those who absent themselves when the church is going through difficult times, since it's in times of pressure that you see a person's true character [2]; inflexibility, where someone is stubborn, unwilling to go beyond what is stipulated, and not prepared to take correction when confronted, as Saul argued with Samuel [3]; and an assistant who is quick to say "I knew all along that this would not work," or who has no comment at all when you bring a new idea or vision [5]. Remember that people will pretend to you and tell you what you want to hear, so a leader must not trust what people are saying wholeheartedly — Jesus did not commit himself to them, because he knew what was in man (John 2:24, 25) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2, 5 and 8 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapter 7 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*.

Scriptures referenced: John 2:24-25; John 7:3; John 7:5.

items.question: What should I read during it?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
You read the Bible — it is the most important book in the world, the most outstanding volume known to the human race, and God's book for us today [1][7]. Read a passage expecting God to speak to you, praying as Psalm 119:18 says, "Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law" [5].

As for what to choose, you can take a book of the Bible and read a few verses every day, always remembering where you stopped so you continue from the same place the next day; the author had wonderful quiet times reading through Luke and Ephesians in the New Testament, and Genesis and 1st and 2nd Samuel in the Old [5]. Or you can follow a personality from the Bible, a few verses about Moses giving much revelation for your life [5]. You may also decide to go through a particular book of the Bible every day, reading a few verses and stopping exactly where the Holy Spirit seems to be speaking — at every word, sentence or phrase that strikes you — then staying there and meditating on it till the full revelation comes [6]. A daily Bible reading guide is also very helpful for developing a regular quiet time habit, and you will benefit from anointed teachers whose ministry helps you grow [4][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills writes about this in chapter 1 of *The Secret*, chapter 3 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day* and chapter 8 of *Key Facts for New Believers*.

items.question: What does it mean to be a shepherd over a small group of people?
items.book: What It Means to Become a Shepherd
items.text:
Being a shepherd over a small group means you see those people as sheep and relate to them as such, caring, loving, guiding and feeding them [1][3][4]. A shepherd is a caring, loving guide to the sheep, someone God has called to look after them [3]. The sheep end up calling their shepherds fathers because of so much loving, caring and guiding [1][6].

It is a great honour to be chosen from among men for this work, to have a job in things pertaining to God, to relate to God directly on behalf of people, and to be chosen to have compassion on the ignorant [2]. You are privileged to help people prosper, to provide good food for the sheep, and to lead them [5]. A shepherd must lead his sheep by still waters and to green pastures, guide them through wilderness situations, and lead them like a flock [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapters 2 and 3 of *The Privilege* and chapter 20 of *The Art of Shepherding*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 23:1-2; Psalms 77:20; Psalms 78:52-54; Psalms 95:6-7; Matthew 9:36; John 21:15-17.

items.question: How should I respond to people who try to turn me against my church leaders?
items.text:
Our books speak plainly to this. Watch out for people who campaign against your fathers, trying to make you turn against your own father [2]. Those who do this are like Absalom, who stole the hearts of the men of Israel from David (2 Samuel 15:6, 15:13) [2]. So be on your guard, and do not be carried along by the story.

At the same time, remember that when a man of God you love is under fire, you should not be offended because of him; it is normal and expected for God's servants to go through fiery trials (Matthew 26:31) [6]. Those who love you will never believe bad things about you [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Those who are Dangerous Sons* and chapter 8 of *Those Who Are Offended*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 15:6; 2 Samuel 15:13; Matthew 26:31.
