items.question: What does the Bible say about people who rebel against their leaders in church?
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this. A rebel is someone who defies and resists authority, openly opposes and disobeys the leader's instructions, and gets into conflict and confrontation with those over him [2]. Scripture takes it seriously: "Rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft" (1 Samuel 15:23), and rebellion is described as a unique sin, distinct from every other [1][7]. The books also say God will not forgive rebellion, citing Joshua 24:19, where He says He "will not forgive your rebellion and your sins" [7][8].

They also warn that rebellion against God's servants is rebellion against God Himself, and that we are to reject and abhor those in rebellion, citing Psalm 139:21 [3]. The Word says to "mark them which cause divisions and offences… and avoid them" (Romans 16:17) [6]. And rebels are described as stubborn men with stiff necks, citing Deuteronomy 31:27 [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapters 1 and 8 of *Those Who Rebel* and chapter 4 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 31:27; Joshua 1:17-18; Joshua 22:19; Joshua 24:19; 1 Samuel 15:23; Nehemiah 9:17; Job 34:37; Psalms 139:21; Proverbs 17:11; Ecclesiastes 1:9 and 1 more.

items.question: What difference does it make whether I serve the Lord or not?
items.book: It Is A Great Thing To Serve The Lord
items.text:
The books say there will always be a difference between those who serve the Lord and those who do not, and that you will return and see it [1]. In the story of the prodigal son, the father said of the son who would not serve in the house, "this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found" (Luke 15:32) — so not serving leaves you lost and dead, while serving means you are found and alive [2].

The differences named are real: a difference in status, since the older brother was a joint heir while the prodigal was no higher than a servant with no rights or standing [3][4]; a difference in covering, since the prodigal had no one to help him [3]; a difference in outcomes, since he became a beggar [3]; and a difference in peace, since he had none in the far country [3]. The father also related differently to each son, telling the faithful servant, "Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine" (Luke 15:31) [2]. And Isaiah warns, "my servants shall eat, but ye shall be hungry... my servants shall rejoice, but ye shall be ashamed" (Isaiah 65:13) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *It Is A Great Thing To Serve The Lord*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 65:12-14; Malachi 3:17-18; Luke 15:15; Luke 15:17; Luke 15:21; Luke 15:29; Luke 15:31-32.

items.question: How does God give revelation to people today if it's not always through visions?
items.text:
Yes, friend, that is a good question, and our books speak to it.

The spirit of revelation does not always come as a vision. John's first revelation was what he called a "real life revelation" — what he had heard, seen, looked upon and touched, the Word of life (1 John 1:1, 3) — and that was just as important as the visions he had later [1]. The spirit of revelation can also lead you to see, hear and know things that few people ever experience [6].

There is another way too: meditation. Most of us will not have those special visions; we will have to depend on meditation, thinking deeply about God's Word, and the lack of meditation is the cause of a lack of personal conviction [7]. And there is blessing simply in believing without seeing — "blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed" (John 20:29) — for many who never had visions, like John Wesley, still bore great fruit [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Victory Secrets*, chapter 30 of *How To Neutralize Curses* and chapter 6 of *Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)*.

Scriptures referenced: John 20:29; Ephesians 1:15-18; 1 Timothy 4:16; 1 John 1:1; 1 John 1:3; Revelation 1:3.

items.question: How do I deal with people in the church who are disloyal or stealing from the offering?
items.text:
Friend, our books speak plainly to both matters.

On disloyal people, the counsel is firm: direct firmness at quieting, humbling, warning and controlling disloyal people [1]. Deal with all disloyal separatists the way God dealt with Satan — throw them out, have no more meetings with them, don't discuss their ideas and visions with them [2]. Disloyal, disobedient or offending workers should be dismissed completely, even longstanding ones, because the real issue is removing unwanted fellowship between you and the offending party [3]. This rests on Proverbs 22:10, "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out" [5][6]. And in keeping with mercy and compassion, financial provisions should be made for longstanding workers so they can live and work elsewhere without undue hardship [3].

On the offering, the books give practical measures: prevent stealing by monitoring who becomes an usher, and keep the ushers in view at all times so none can dip their fingers into the offering bags [7][8]. Have two or three people count the money at the same time, never leave anyone alone with it, use a signed form that corresponds with the bank pay-in slips, keep it in a secure safe, and bank 100% of it promptly [7][8]. Offerings should not be kept in the pastor's house, lest he be accused of misusing the church's money [7][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *A Good General*, chapter 12 of *One of You is a Devil*, chapter 77 of *The Gift Of Governments*, chapter 8 of *Pillars of Loyalty*, chapter 10 of *Church Growth* and chapter 3 of *Church Administration*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 15:11; Proverbs 22:10; Titus 1:5; Hebrews 12:15.

items.question: What happens to a person who dies without being born again?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak plainly to this. When you die you will either go to Heaven or Hell — you will not just stop existing, but head for a permanent destination away from this earth [4]. The rich man in Luke 16 died and in hell he lifted up his eyes, being in torments, while Lazarus was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom [4].

The reason is that sin came into the world through one man, and death as the result of sin spread to all men because all sinned (Romans 5:12), so that every unsaved soul is bound to end up in hell [2]. Unless a man is born again spiritually and reconciled to God through Christ, he is headed for Hell [2]. It is the soul that goes to Hell; your spirit and your soul will suffer there [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *People Who Went to Hell* and chapters 3 and 4 of *How to be Born again & Avoid Hell*.

Scriptures referenced: Jeremiah 17:9; Mark 8:36; Luke 16:19-31; Romans 1:18; Romans 5:12.
